Bio: Anya is Senior Lecturer in Philosophy and Ethics in the School of Humanities, University of Tasmania. Interdisciplinary collaborations are at the core of Anya’s research interests. She investigates the intersections of phenomenology with philosophy of mind, the philosophy of perception, the philosophy of psychiatry, embodied and social cognition, enactivism, ethics, aesthetics and Buddhist Philosophy. Anya has received funding from national and international institutions to support her research projects and also to facilitate the dissemination of her own work and the work of others through publications, organising workshops and conferences. Notable among these was The Inhuman Gaze, a three-day multi-disciplinary international conference spanning the disciplines of philosophy, cognitive neuroscience, psychiatry, psychology, sociology and aesthetics, which was hosted in Paris 2018 - https://theinhumangaze.com/. Papers from this conference were published by Routledge in an edited volume for which she was the chief editor. https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/edit/10.4324/9780367815707/perception-inhuman-gaze-dermot-moran-fred-cummins-anya-daly-james-jardineShe has published in ethics, aesthetics, philosophy of psychiatry, feminism, social cognition, philosophy of psychology, philosophy of perception, ontology and animal ethics.Anya completed a double-badged doctorate (en-cotutelle) between Université de Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne et University of Melbourne in December 2012.She has taught in programs at undergraduate and graduate levels at the University of Melbourne, Sciences Po Paris, ESSEC Paris, University Lyon 3, University College Dublin, Monash University - European philosophy, Anglo-American philosophy, history of ideas, epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, business ethics, management ethics, aesthetics, history and philosophy of psychiatry, and philosophy of science.Anya spent five years researching and teaching in France (2005-2010) under the supervision of Professor Renaud Barbaras, and two years in Dublin at University College Dublin under the mentorship of Professor Dermot Moran, on an Irish Research Council Fellowship (2016-2018). In the years 2010 - 2016, and 2018 - 2021 she was based at the University of Melbourne. Now she is based at the University of Tasmania at the Inveresk campus.

Bio: Dr Bennet McComish is a Senior Research Fellow in the Menzies Institute for Medical Research at the University of Tasmania. He leads the Evolutionary Medicine group within the MS Research Flagship.Bennet's background is in molecular evolution and bioinformatics, and he currently leads a team investigating the evolutionary origins of genetic risk factors for multiple sclerosis. This work includes scanning human genome data for signatures of natural selection (including local adaptation) and modeling evolutionary processes such as admixture and genetic drift. He has worked across a range of complex diseases, including multiple sclerosis and inherited eye diseases. He manages a dedicated genomics high-performance computing cluster, supporting and training research staff and students who use the cluster. His work involves analysing genome sequence data using bioinformatic tools to identify the genetic variants that are most likely to be involved in causing disease.Bennet completed a PhD in Computational Biology in the Allan Wilson Centre for Molecular Ecology and Evolution (New Zealand). He joined the School of Mathematics and Physics at the University of Tasmania in 2013 as a postdoctoral researcher investigating the evolutionary dynamics of microsatellite sequences, before moving to his current position at the Menzies in 2016.

Research fields: Genomics, Molecular evolution, Phylogeny and comparative analysis, Genetics, Biological sciences, Evolutionary biology

Bio: Bethany Wilkinson is a Senior Lecturer at the University of Tasmania, Australia. She is primarily concerned with supporting the realisation of social justice for women who experience male perpetrated intimate partner violence. Bethany has a particular interest in developing a cohesive understanding of intimate partner violence across a variety of disciplines with the aim integrating feminist knowledges into system responses. Her most recent work explores women’s agency in recovering from intimate partner violence in all dimensions of their lives: health, recreation, friendship, work or career, family and nourishing and supportive intimate partnership.

Bio: Dr Brooklyn Fraser is a Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Research Fellow. Her research is focused on the health and fitness of Australian children, with a strong interest in the long-term cardiovascular health benefits of greater fitness.

Brooklyn completed a Bachelor of Biotechnology and Medical Research with First Class Honours in 2015. Brooklyn received her PhD from the University of Tasmania in 2019. Brooklyn’s PhD explored the association between childhood muscular fitness and type 2 diabetes related outcomes in adulthood. Her research helped identify muscular fitness, in childhood and across the life course, as a target to help prevent type 2 diabetes. Brooklyn was awarded the Menzies Institute for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship in 2020 and a nationally competitive Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship in 2022. Brooklyn’s postdoctoral research examines the health and fitness of Australian children, with a strong focus on the long-term cardiovascular health benefits of greater fitness.

Brooklyn works with large observational studies with longitudinal data and is experienced with analytic techniques relevant to longitudinal data including life-course modelling. Brooklyn has independently developed highly engaged, impactful and ongoing international collaborations with leading paediatric exercise science experts, formalised within the Global Youth Fitness Consortium (>100 international collaborators).

Brooklyn's research vision is to establish and champion the protective power of childhood fitness to enable children to lead fit and heart-healthy lives into adulthood. She aims for her research to inform public health and clinical guidelines, early prevention strategies, and school‑based programs that strengthen child fitness.

Bio: I am a Senior Lecturer in International Relations in the School of Social Sciences at the University of Tasmania. Prior to this, I was Senior Lecturer and Course Coordinator at the University of Sussex, and Associate Professor and Head of International Studies at the University of Nottingham Ningbo, China. I am author of the textbook 'World Politics. A Critical Introduction'.
My academic trajectory has been shaped by a cosmopolitan background: I have studied and worked in five countries, across two continents, and in three languages. This lived experience informs my commitment to critical approaches in International Relations. My research and teaching are driven by the conviction that decolonising, indigenising, and feminising the discipline are not only matters of justice but also of intellectual integrity. I seek to challenge dominant narratives in order to generate new ways of understanding global politics and our place within it.
In addition to my academic work, I maintain a broad range of interests, from kendo and kayaking to bushwalking and textile crafts, and I am also a mother of two.

Bio: Dr Charlotte Dunn is a Senior Lecturer in Classics in the School of Humanities and Social Science. Charlotte’s research areas include the Age of Alexander the Great and the Hellenistic Age, with a particular focus on the lives and careers of the Successors who rose to power after Alexander’s death to form empires of their own. One of the major subjects of Charlotte’s research is the colourful Demetrius ‘the Besieger’ Poliorcetes, and she co-authored the first full-length monograph on the life of this infamous Hellenistic king, Demetrius the Besieger (2020).Her research expertise also includes the use of political imagery and propaganda in the Ancient World, the development of the Hellenistic royal dynasties and their family dynamics, historiography, medical humanities, as well as the field of numismatics.BiographyBefore joining the University of Tasmania, Charlotte studied at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand where she completed her undergraduate and postgraduate degrees, in Classics, Greek and Latin. Bio: Dr Claire Eccleston is a Senior Lecturer in Dementia Care in the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. She has a keen interest in dementia education and literacy, and in health literacy and how it can be supported by health workers. She brings experience in quantitative and mixed methods research relating to the assessment of knowledge, attitudes, and health literacy about dementia and dementia risk reduction. She has developed and validated a number of related survey instruments, and has supported their translation into many different languages. She has a breadth of experience in evaluating the effectiveness of education across multiple modes such as massive open online courses, online undergraduate courses, training of health and care professionals, and clinical placements. BiographyDr Eccleston has a PhD in quantitative ecology from Griffith University, Queensland. After returning to Tasmania, she worked part time as a Research Fellow on the Wicking Teaching Aged Care Facilities Program from 2011 to 2015, leading the evaluation component of the second part of this program between 2013-2015. The program aimed to prototype Teaching Aged Care Facilities by providing healthcare students with a quality clinical placement in residential aged care. Dr Eccleston’s work has included the development, validation and translation of a number of validated and psychometrically sound scales to investigate dementia knowledge (DKAS), dementia literacy (CAAASI-Dem), dementia risk reduction knowledge (KoDeRR), and public dementia stigma (DePSS). Claire has been a full-time lecturer with the Dementia Care degree program since 2016, and was Course coordinator of the Bachelor and Diploma of Dementia Care from July 2020- December 2023. In 2017, Claire led an investigation of dementia knowledge and education needs in the Tasmanian community and since then has been a member of teams investigating the attitudes, experiences and knowledge needs of the current and future health and care workforce. She is currently an investigator on multiple projects such as a major project to increase awareness of traumatic brain injury and the ISLAND project which aims to understand how we can promote behavioural change to reduce risk of dementia, as well as a project exploring health literacy responsiveness in the University's health and care students.Qualifications PhD, Griffith University, Australia, 2005. Role: Doctor

Bio: Damien Kingston is a Hobart-born guitarist, composer, researcher, and educator whose practice spans performance, recording, curriculum leadership, and community engagement across jazz, improvised music, and contemporary creative practice. After completing a Bachelor of Music at the University of Tasmania, Damien relocated to Europe, working as a freelance musician and completing a Masters of Music at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam (2013) under Dutch guitar luminaries Martijn van Iterson and Jesse van Ruller, following an active period in Berlin's jazz and improvised music community.

Returning to Tasmania, Damien completed a PhD at the University of Tasmania (2018) and joined the Conservatorium as a casual lecturer in 2014 before moving to ongoing employment in 2019. He currently holds three formal leadership positions - Associate Head Learning and Teaching, Course Coordinator, and Honours Coordinator - with accountability for the Bachelor of Music, Diploma of Music, Associate Degree, and Honours award courses. His teaching philosophy integrates academic rigour, industry authenticity, and inclusive practice, supporting students from diverse backgrounds to develop professional skills and discover their own artistic voice.

As a performer and recording artist, Damien has released seven albums of original compositions and contributed to more than thirty commercial releases across jazz, experimental, and contemporary popular music. His 2021 ABC-commissioned album Wells reached audiences across more than one hundred countries and was selected as Album of the Week on ABC Jazz Radio. His most recent release, Let the Light In - Damien Kingston Quartet (2023), was released by Made Now Music. Damien has performed internationally both as a bandleader and sideman, and received awards including first place in the 2016 Berlin Jazz & Blues Awards and a finalist placement in the 2013 Keep an Eye European Jazz Awards.

Beyond the institution, Damien is a committed builder of Tasmania's creative ecosystem - founding the Pablo's Jazz Jam Session (now in its seventh year), co-founding Scratch Match Records, leading the Conservatorium's partnership with the Clarence Jazz Festival.

Bio: David is a marine spatial ecologist and Lecturer in Marine Spatial Ecology at IMAS (Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies), University of Tasmania. With around 15 years of experience in biologging and animal tracking, he has worked across more than 15 marine predator species, spanning temperate, Subantarctic and Antarctic systems. His research combines biotelemetry, statistical and mechanistic modelling approaches to resolve links between the physical environment and ecological processes across multiple trophic levels, from oceanographic drivers through mid trophic prey dynamics to top predator foraging ecology. He holds a PhD from IMAS, a strong publication record built over more than a decade, and extensive field leadership experience, including coordinating tagging voyages and expeditions across remote and polar systems. His work increasingly bridges research and policy, contributing to international spatial conservation and management processes, alongside a growing teaching, supervision, and mentorship portfolio.

Supervisor: Doctor Elly Quinlan

Role: Doctor

Bio: I'm a psychologist (clinical, educational & developmental), senior lecturer, and supervisor with a focus on professional training, ethics, and inclusive practice. I've contributed to the development and review of postgraduate psychology programs across several institutions. I teach into postgraduate psychology, supervise both research and clinical placements, and support students as they navigate the realities of becoming a psychologist. I particularly value working closely with students as they develop their professional identity and confidence.
My research focuses on strengthening the structures and supports that shape postgraduate psychology training and professional practice. I've explored areas such as practicum logbooks, sexual abuse inquiry, fostering tolerance of uncertainty, supporting students experiencing competency issues, and the development of mentoring programs. I also have research interests in neurodiversity and neurodivergence, role-play and gaming, recovery-oriented approaches, and the experiences of mental health carers.A consistent focus of my work is translating research into practical resources and guidance that can be used in training and professional settings.
Clinically, I have worked with young people experiencing trauma, attachment disruptions, grief and loss, sexual abuse, disability, and neurodivergence, and I am particularly committed to neuroaffirming and trauma-informed approaches.
Outside the university, I serve as Deputy Chair of the Psychology Board of Australia’s Registration and Compliance Committee, am a member of the Australian Psychology Accreditation Council Stakeholder Reference Group, and serve as Associate Editor of Australian Psychologist.. I also work as a Witness Intermediary in the Tasmanian justice system, supporting vulnerable witnesses to participate fairly in legal proceedings.
As a neurodivergent person, I'm particularly attuned to the ways systems can either support or exclude- and I'm committed to building professional spaces that are more transparent, inclusive, and compassionate.I supervise research at the Masters and PhD level and welcome discussions with potential research candidates.

Research fields: Child and adolescent development, Educational psychology, Clinical and health psychology, Curriculum and pedagogy, Applied and developmental psychology, Psychology, Education

Supervisor: Doctor Emiliano Cimoli

Role: Doctor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Ecology and Biodiversity

Bio: Emiliano's work advances remote sensing applications for mapping the biogeochemical properties of aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. He is particularly interested in retrieving fine-scale environmental attributes and understanding how they shape larger-scale ecosystem dynamics.Dr Cimoli completed his PhD at the Institute of Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) of the University of Tasmania (UTAS) working on the development of underwater hyperspectral imaging and photogrammetric techniques to map keystone Antarctic ice algal ecosystems. He has worked at the Australian Centre of Excellence in Antarctic Science (ACEAS) to design a portable acustically aided-Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) to monitor biogeochemical linkages between benthic and sympagic Antarctica coastal under-ice environments.Following his PhD, Emiliano pursued a postdoctoral research fellowship at the TerraLuma Research group as part of the Australian Research Council (ARC) Discovery project “Ultrahigh-resolution remote sensing for assessing biodiversity hotspots”. Within TerraLuma, a world-leading group in the field of remote sensing from Unoccupied Aerial Systems (UAS), he has honed his skills in a range of terrestrial applications at the forefront of sensor and algorithm development for hyperspectral image georectification and plant (functional) biodiversity monitoring.

Dr. Cimoli was awarded a prestigious JSPS Postdoctoral Fellowship from the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science in November 2024 to collaborate with Hokkaido University, where he investigates Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR) imaging solutions to quantify cryogenic mineral formation within sea ice. His research integrates hyperspectral imaging and sea-ice biogeochemistry, contributing to advancements in the interactions between sea ice, phytoplankton, and carbon fluxes in polar oceans.
Before joining the University of Tasmania, Emiliano consolidated a strong civil and environmental engineering background through both his BSc (University of Padua, Italy) and MSc (Technical University of Denmark) to then specialize in the fields of optical remote sensing and geomatics. He has worked considerably in both the Arctic and Antarctic and several other remote locations providing him also an enhanced logistics and engineering background. His experiences range from technical equipment design and set-up, data acquisition, data processing and analysis up to workflow implementation and academic and public dissemination.

Role: Doctor

Bio: Gabi Mocatta is a communication and journalism researcher who currently studies communicational responses to climate change. This multifocal work takes place at the site where climate change science, public understanding and collective discourse on climate change and environmental policy intersect. Gabi also examines media representations of climate change - given most people derive their understanding of our changing climate from the media. She additionally researches climate literacy, to better understand what spurs climate action at all levels of society. Gabi is currently Senior Research Fellow in Climate Science Communication with the globally-known Climate Futures Research Group in the School of Geography, Planning and Spatial Sciences.A former journalist, Gabi began her academic career at the University of Tasmania teaching journalism. She undertook her PhD in environmental communication at the university's Media School. Gabi then worked as Lecturer in Communication and Course Director of the Masters in Communication at Deakin University, Melbourne. She has been a member of the Climate Futures research group since 2020, bringing expertise in climate communication and climate science translation for public policy making and behaviour change. Climate Futures works with with a wide range of industry and government stakeholders to deliver climate information for preparedness and adaptation.Gabi collaborates on several projects related to promoting climate literacy and action. She has worked with local government to understand and deliver climate projection needs, and to provide climate science translation for community. She also investigates the role of communication in responding to natural hazards and is a research leader for Natural Hazards Research Australia. She is also part of the team that delivers the award winning Curious Climate Schools climate literacy program for young people. Internationally, Gabi collaborates with the Media and Climate Change Observatory at the University of Colorado, Boulder, as part of the team led by Prof. Max Boykoff. This project traces media coverage of climate change around the world since 2000.

She has been president of the International Environmental Communication Association (2023-2025) and in 2025 she was elected as vice-Chair, progressing to Chair, of the International Communication Association's Environmental Communication Division.

Gabi is an Associate Deputy Editor of the journal Climatic Change.

Supervisor: Doctor Gabriela Bodea

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Gabriela Bodea is a Senior Lecturer in Biomedicine and Head of the Molecular Neurogenetics Lab at the Tasmanian School of Medicine, University of Tasmania.

Dr Bodea completed her PhD with the highest distinction, summa cum laude, at the University of Bonn (2014, Germany). Dr Bodea subsequently pursued postdoctoral training at the Mater Research Institute and then at the Queensland Brain Institute, University of Queensland, Australia. During this time, Dr Bodea's work significantly contributed to understanding the role of LINE-1 retrotransposons, a class of mobile DNA elements colloquially known as “jumping genes” in generating genetic diversity within neurons during mammalian neurodevelopment (Cell, 2015; Genome Research 2017, 2022, 2023; Nature Neuroscience, 2024). In mid-2025, Dr Bodea relocated to the University of Tasmania, assuming a teaching and research role and establishing the Molecular Neurogenetics Research Lab.

Dr Bodea's Molecular Neurogenetics (MNG) Research Lab investigates the mechanisms of neural plasticity, specifically how environmental exposures shape the genetic identity of neurons and direct the formation of mammalian brain circuitry, enabling adaptive processes. The MNG team also aims to understand how environmental factors, immune signalling, and genetic predisposition contribute to complex neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative conditions, such as schizophrenia and Parkinson’s disease. To address these questions, the MNG team applies a powerful, integrated toolkit spanning cellular and molecular biology, neuroscience, and genomics. This multidisciplinary approach enables the MNG team to precisely dissect gene-regulatory mechanisms and delineate the cellular and molecular pathways that drive vulnerability and resilience in the central nervous system.

Our research has secured prestigious and highly competitive funding, including fellowships from the German Research Foundation (DFG, 2014-2016), the NHMRC-ARC Dementia Research Development (2016-2020), and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation (BBRF) Young Investigator Award (2025-2027). Reflecting the impact of our work, our findings have been published in top-tier journals, including Nature Neuroscience, Cell Reports, Genome Research, and Development.

Methods and Techniques of the Molecular Neurogenetics Lab

Mouse models (transgene, conditional gene inactivation and overexpression via CRISPRi/a, genetic inducible fate mapping)
Histology (paraffin- and cryosectioning, RNA in situ hybridisation, immunohistochemistry)
Cell culture (induced pluripotent stem cells, primary neuronal cultures, organotypic slice culture, organoid and assembloid 3D cultures)
Genomics and transcriptomics (RNAseq, DNA and RNA long-read sequencing)
Epigenetic tools (CUT&RUN, CUT&Tag)
Molecular biology (PCR, RNA and DNA analysis, gene cloning, qPCR)
Microscopy (confocal microscopy, fluorescence live imaging)

Research fields: Neurogenetics, Cellular nervous system, Animal cell and molecular biology, Molecular targets, Epigenetics (incl. genome methylation and epigenomics), Animal neurobiology, Genetics, Biological sciences, Neurosciences, Biomedical and clinical sciences, Zoology, Oncology and carcinogenesis

Bio: Dr. Gary Morris is a lecturer within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. He completed his PhD in 2017 at the University of New South Wales, before undertaking postdoctoral research at University of Technology, Sydney, from 2017-2019.

In 2019, Dr. Morris joined the Perivascular Research Group at the University of Tasmania, led by Professor Brad Sutherland, as a Research Fellow. During this time he worked on projects related to comparative neuroanatomy, physiological neurovascular function, stroke, Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia and multiple sclerosis.

In 2025, Dr. Morris began his research group, the Gliovascular Research Group, within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre at UTAS. His research investigates how non-neuronal cells residing within the brain, and around the vasculature of the brain, contribute to vascular functions including the control of brain blood flow, blood-brain-barrier protection and brain waste removal. His research aims to understand how the gliovascular unit functions in the healthy brain, but also how it breaks down and thereby contributes to microvascular dysfunction in multiple neurological conditions, with a focus on dementia and stroke.

Dr. Morris teaches into several undergraduate neuroscience and biochemistry units within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre and the Tasmanian School of Medicine. He also supervises several postgraduate research students.

Bio: Greg is an evolutionary ecologist that seeks to answer fundamental questions in ecology and evolution that improve our understanding of how biodiversity is created, and how populations cope with novel environments. As a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Bristol (2017-2020), he tested mechanisms that promote persistence in novel environments by conducting large-scale field experiments in Sicily using seeds and clones of two species of Senecio wildflowers. For his DECRA fellowship at Monash University (2020-2024), he used laboratory experiments to identify the mechanisms that help populations to maintain ecological resilience in response to stressful environments representing climate change scenarios. His current research goals are to understand how plants evolve to buffer environmental variation that includes climate extremes and apply this knowledge to develop climate-resilient crops through collaboration with plant breeders and Indigenous communities.

Bio: Dr. Hannah Fair has two overlapping focuses: the role of social networks in dementia risk reduction, and understanding and improving equity in health promotion, particularly in dementia prevention. She evaluates online health education programs like the ISLAND project Linking Aging and Neurodegenerative Disease, and the Preventing Dementia Massive Open Online Course, to assessing their impact and reach through mixed-methods research. Dr. Fair also explores the role of social networks in transmitting dementia risk information and behaviour, and is increasingly interested in the broader role of social networks in promoting dementia risk reducing behaviour. Her research methods involve both quantitative (statistical modelling, social network analysis) and qualitative (interviews, focus groups, thematic analysis) approaches. She teaches on public health approaches to dementia and dementia risk reduction, emphasizing health equity and social determinants of health. Dr. Hannah Fair works for the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre at the University of Tasmania, and welcomes any and all conversations with individuals who share her interests.

Bio: Dr Hongyuan Liu is currently a senior lecturer in geomechanics at the School of Engineering in the College of Sciences and Engineering, University of Tasmania and an affiliated research scientist at CSIRO Mineral Resources. Hong's research interest is in the field of geohazard mitigation and prevention, computational geomechanics, tunnelling, and rock mechanics. In particular, Hong's research focuses on the development and application of advanced computational methods such as hybrid finite-discrete element method (HFDEM) in studying the fracture and fragmentation of rocks under various static and dynamic loads during tunnelling and mining, associated microseismicities, and their interactions with underground fluids such as groundwater, oil, gas and hazardous waste as well as mitigating and even preventing geohazards such as rockbursts, slope instabilities and iceberg calving. For example, Hong recently developed HFDEM and founded its website: https://sites.google.com/view/hfdem/home. Together with his team, Hong parallelised HFDEM on the basis of general-purpose graphic-processing-units (GPGPU) using compute unified device architecture (CUDA) C/C++ and developed a number of novel and efficient features, which have made HFDEM become a powerful numerical tool for investigating the fracture and fragmentation of rocks under static and dynamic loading conditions as well as mitigating and preventing the instability and collapse of rockmass structures and resultant debris fragmentation and flow process. Hong's and his team's series of research on the development and application of HFDEM has claimed a series of awards including the Top 15 Highest Ranked Paper in the 12th Australia - New Zealand Conference on Geomechanics in 2012, the Best PhD Student Paper Awards in the 3rd and 4th Australasian Conference on Computational Mechanics in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the only Excellent Paper Award in the 5th ISRM Young Scholar's Symposium on Rock Mechanics and International Symposium on Rock Engineering for Innovative Future in 2019 and the Excellent Paper Award in the 11th Asian Rock Mechanics Symposium in 2020. HFDEM is free to use for the purpose of research and/or verification although the use of the code for military and commercial purpose is prohibited. If interested, please download HFDEM and know more information from our website: https://sites.google.com/view/hfdem/home. Hong's research has resulted in more than 100 peer-reviewed journal papers including many in the leading geomechanics journals such as International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences, Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering, and Computers and Geotechnics, which have attracted a citation number of 3088 and 4111 citations and an h-index of 32 and 36 according to Scopus and Google Scholar, respectively, till June 2023.BiographyDr Hongyuan Liu's current research at UTAS encompasses the broad areas of geohazard mitigation and prevention, computational geomechanics, tunnelling and rock mechanics. He is the academic manager of Geomechanics Lab at UTAS and teaches ENG221 Engineering Geology and Soil Mechanics, ENG315/706 Foundation Engineering and Design and ENG717 Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering.Hong was a research fellow at the Golder Geomechanics Centre led by Prof David Williams within the University of Queensland before being appointed in UTAS in 2010. Prior to joining in UQ in 2008, Hong was a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Sydney funded by an ARC Discovery Project 'Effects of Tunnelling on Existing Support System' held by Profs John Small and John Carter. Hong completed his PhD at Lulea University of Technology, Sweden in 2004 and later worked there as a research scientist till moving to Australia in 2006. During the period as a research scientist, Hong, together with Profs Per-Arne Lindqvist and SQ Kou, attracted research grants of over $1M SEK from LKAB, Atlas Copco, SKB's Aspo Hard Rock Laboratory and SGU. Prior to being awarded PhD scholarships by LTU Sweden in 2001, Hong completed his Masters and Bachelor degrees at Northeastern University China in 2000 and 1997, respectively, during which, he was the early developer of the RFPA code led by Cheung Kong Professor Tang.Career summaryQualifications2004: PhD, Lulea University of Technology, Sweden 20042000: ME, Northeastern University, China1997: BE, Northeastern University, China 1997Languages (other than English)Chinese, SwedishMemberships:Committee associationsFellow of Institute of Engineers AustraliaMember of International Society of Rock MechanicsMember of Australian Geomechanics SocietyMember of Australian Institute of Mining and MetallurgyEditorial Board Members of International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Science, Underground Space and other 3 SCI-indexed journalsRegular peer reviewer for more than 10 international journals including International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences, Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering, Computers and Geotechnics, and Tunnelling and Underground Space Technology

Bio: Dr Jane Younger is a Senior Lecturer in Southern Ocean Vertebrate Ecology at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS). Her research integrates an Antarctic field program with cutting edge multi-omics approaches to monitor the complex impacts of climate change on Antarctic biodiversity, with a particular focus on understanding the threat of disease to wildlife in a changing environment. She is a 2025-26 Science and Technology Australia Superstar of STEM, a Senior Editor of Ecology and Evolution, a National Geographic Explorer, and a 2025 Young Tall Poppy Award winner.Prior to joining IMAS in 2022, Jane was a research fellow in the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath (UK). Her research focused on understanding the impacts of climate change on seabirds, through an evolutionary lens. She has also held an Endeavour Fellowship at the University of Oxford (UK) where she used genomics to examine the population structure of Southern Ocean penguin species. Prior to that she held a postdoctoral position at Loyola University Chicago (USA) and in affiliation with the Field Museum of Natural History, studying the evolution of Madagascar’s endemic avifauna. Jane completed her PhD in 2016 at IMAS, where she focused on the past impacts of climate change on Southern Ocean marine predators.

Jane’s published work spans the fields of ecology, conservation, evolution, genomics, and wildlife health. The common theme throughout her career has been understanding how environmental change effects biodiversity.

Supervisor: Doctor Jayne Knight

Role: Doctor

School: School of Humanities

Sub-organisation: History and Classics

Bio: Dr Jayne Knight is Senior Lecturer in Classics and Associate Head of School, Learning and Teaching Performance in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. She researches the emotional culture of ancient Rome, with a particular focus on how emotions shaped politics and rhetoric in the late Republic and early Empire. Her monograph Anger and Politics in Ancient Rome (Bloomsbury, 2026) is the centrepiece of this program, building on her earlier work including ‘Anger as a Mechanism for Social Control in Imperial Rome’ in Emotion and Persuasion in Classical Antiquity (Franz Steiner Verlag, 2016), and connecting with forthcoming chapters on ‘Emotions in Roman Oratory’ in A Companion to Ancient Rhetoric: New Trends and Interdisciplinary Perspectives (De Gruyter, expected 2026) and ‘Senecan Strategies for Managing Envy in Early Imperial Rome’ for a planned volume on Envy in the Roman World (University of Michigan Press). Her entries on ‘emotions’ and ‘hatred’ in The Tacitus Encyclopedia (Wiley-Blackwell, 2023) further reflect her interest in the affective dimensions of Roman historical writing.

A second strand of her research examines how Roman thought on politics and emotions was received and transformed in later periods. Her ARC-funded project on Machiavelli's engagement with Roman political theory informs a forthcoming chapter on ‘Anger and Discord in Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy’ in Machiavelli and the Anatomy of Passions (Brill). Her chapter ‘The Nature and Nurture of Kingship in Virgil's Georgics and Seneca's De Clementia’ in Latin Poetry and its Reception (Routledge, 2021) analyses Seneca's engagement with earlier Virgilian ideas and imagery to activate historical memory.

Jayne believes that ancient texts speak to deep questions of human life, and one of the most rewarding things Classics can do is help students experience and appreciate the deep connections and gulfs between the ancient world and their own. She has taught ancient Roman history and culture and Latin language units at all levels. Her commitment to expanding access for students has driven sustained innovation in blended and online learning, recognised by multiple University of Tasmania Teaching Merit Certificates, a Student Focus Award, and a Team Citation for Outstanding Contributions to Student Learning. She has also contributed extensively to curriculum development at unit, major, and course level, including serving as Course Coordinator for the Bachelor of Arts with Honours and Assistant Dean, Distinctiveness and Innovation in the former College of Arts, Law and Education.

Jayne is passionate about bringing the ancient world into public conversation, whether discussing Roman political culture, the lives of ancient people, or the ways that classical antiquity continues to shape how we think in the present. Alongside writing for general audiences in venues such as The Conversation and History Today, Jayne regularly gives public lectures and talks for community organisations, universities, and online audiences in Australia and internationally.

Research fields: Latin and classical Greek literature, Classical Greek and Roman history, Literary studies, Language, communication and culture, Historical studies, History, heritage and archaeology

Supervisor: Doctor Jessica Urwin

Role: Doctor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: School of Humanities and Social Sciences

Bio: Jessica Urwin is Lecturer in Environmental History in the School of Humanities, College of Arts, Law and Education. Her research interests and expertise span nuclear history, Australian history, environmental history, colonial and imperial history, and environmental justice. Her award-winning doctoral research, completed at the Australian National University, explored the relationship between nuclear processes (including radium and uranium mining, nuclear weapons testing, and nuclear waste dumping) and colonialism in Australia. Her first monograph, Contaminated Country: Nuclear Colonialism and Aboriginal Resistance in Australia, was published in the University of Washington Press' Weyehaeuser Environmental Books series in September 2025 and an Australian edition is set to be published by Melbourne University Press in 2026.

Jess is a member of the Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand Environmental History Network's steering committee, an editorial board member of Global Environment, and a Friend of the Centre for Environmental History at ANU.

Research Interests

Jess' research interests span across Australian scientific, environmental, political, and colonial history. Her immediate field of expertise is in Australian nuclear, colonial, and environmental histories, but she has also worked on historical research concerned with the Murray-Darling Basin and other 'watery spaces', oral history, global environmental history, and the history of science and scientific networks in Australia and beyond.

Expanding upon her work into nuclear colonialism, Jess is interested in Australian mining history, and hopes to engage critically with the industry's environmental and colonial dimensions, from settlement through to the present. In particular, she is interested in the politics of mineral extraction, from understanding the 'roots' of settlers' engagements with mining (in particular of radioactive minerals), to tracing the 'routes' of mined minerals across the world, to grappling with mining's more recent interactions with Indigenous land rights and conservation debates.

Teaching Summary

Jess is passionate about providing inclusive and accessible education to her students. She has taught global imperial history, Australian colonial history, and global environmental history, and provided mentorship to undergraduate, Honours and PhD students. She is the current coordinator of HASS Honours, and unit coordinator of HUM410: Contemporary Humanities Research, HUM405: Advanced Reading Seminar, HUM419: Advanced Text-Based Reading Seminar, HAA106: Oral History, and HTA348: Global Environmental History (alongside A/Prof Alessandro Antonello).

Research fields: Environmental history, Australian history, History of empires, imperialism and colonialism, Historical studies, History, heritage and archaeology

Bio: Dr Johanna Jones is a postdoctoral researcher at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research. After working in the education sector for several years, Johanna undertook additional study to complement her interests in health and human disease. She has a great interest in understanding how genetic variants disrupt normal cell biology and lead to disease. Johanna’s research is primarily focused on the genetics of childhood onset (congenital/paediatric) cataracts. She was awarded a PhD in 2020 from the University of Tasmania in the genetics of paediatric cataract. This successful body of work identified PGRMC1 as a novel isolated cataract gene, expanded the genotype-phenotype spectrum of known cataract genes, and has initiated investigations into the importance of structural and non-coding variants in cataract genetics. Johanna has honed a broad range of skills from sequencing and bioinformatics for variant identification and prioritisation, through numerous molecular biology techniques and use of zebrafish as a cataract disease model for variant validation and functional assessments. Johanna is also interested in developing in vitro assays to test the functional effects of putative disease-causing variants to improve genetic testing outcomes for patients. Johanna is passionate about undertaking research that will benefit patients and improve health outcomes for individuals with genetic diseases.

Supervisor: Doctor Juan Afonso

Role: Doctor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: Earth Sciences/CODES

Bio: A/Prof. Juan C. Afonso's background is in computational geoscience and geodata integration. After graduating with a PhD in theoretical geophysics at Carleton University, Juan C. Afonso undertook postdoctoral research at the Institute of Earth Sciences Jaume Almera (CSIC, Barcelona) on the development of new methods to study the thermal and compositional structures of the lithospheric/sublithospheric upper mantle. He subsequently joined Macquarie University in 2009 as part of the recruitment program CoRE (Concentration of Research Excellence). In 2022, he joined the ITC Faculty (University of Twente, Netherlands) as full-time staff. In 2026 he joined the School of Natural Sciences at the University of Tasmania. He was an Adjunct Professor at the Centre for Earth Evolution and Dynamics (CEED, University of Oslo) and Honorary Professor at the Dept. of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Macquarie University. He currently is a Visiting Professor in the Department of Earth and Space Sciences at SUSTech University and in ITC at the University of Twente.

Dr Afonso's current research includes the development of methodologies (and associated computational tools) that formally combine geophysics, numerical modelling, petrology and geochemistry to obtain reliable and realistic models of the Earth's interior using satellite-derived and land-based data sets. For this (and related) work he has received the 2013 EGU Outstanding Young Scientist Award (Geodynamics Division), the 2017 Anton Hales Medal of the Australian Academy of Sciences and the 2019 IUGG Early Career Scientist Award, among others.

His research centers on understanding the thermochemical structure and evolution of the lithosphere, as well as the mechanical and geochemical interactions between tectonic plates and the sublithospheric upper mantle. His work explores how these interactions influence both regional and global tectonic processes, with implications for plate dynamics, mantle convection, and crustal evolution.
​​
His most recent research integrates machine learning, multiscale probabilistic inversion, and numerical modeling to investigate some of the most fundamental questions about the nature and evolution of the lithosphere and upper mantle using a formal combination of multiple satellite (e.g. gravity, magnetic field) and land-based (e.g. geochemistry, seismic) data sets.
​​
He also works on the development of novel numerical algorithms to model the complex coupling between geodynamic and geochemical processes. This work directly supports the global energy transition by enabling more accurate and physically realistic models for geothermal resource assessment and critical mineral exploration. His methodologies assist in identifying subsurface conditions favorable for sustainable energy development and securing the raw materials essential for clean energy technologies.

Currently, Dr. Afonso is the leader and coordinator of the following large projects:
​
- The EU Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network EarthSafe: Unveiling Earth's Critical Resources for Clean Energy and a Sustainable Future (https://earthsafe-dn.eu/)
​
- The passive seismic experiment PatagoniARRAY (imaging and modelling the Patagonian lithosphere)
​
- The NWO DeepNL Project INTEGRATION (Integrated subsurface modelling beneath Groningen and on-shore Netherlands from multi-data probabilistic inversions; link)
​
He also enjoys very much spending quality time with his family and playing drums whenever possible...

Supervisor: Doctor Karelle Siellez

Role: Doctor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: Physics

Bio: Dr Karelle Siellez is an astrophysicist and Lecturer in Physics at the University of Tasmania. Her research focuses on transient and multi-messenger astrophysics, including gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae, supernovae, gravitational-wave counterparts, and rapid optical follow-up of short-lived cosmic explosions. Her work connects high-energy space missions, gravitational-wave observatories, and ground-based telescope networks to understand some of the most energetic events in the Universe.
Before joining UTAS, Dr Siellez contributed to major international collaborations including LIGO/Virgo and Fermi/GBM. She developed and led work on subthreshold gamma-ray burst searches associated with gravitational-wave events, contributing to the scientific context of the first joint gravitational-wave and electromagnetic detection, GW170817/GRB 170817A. This discovery transformed the field by confirming that neutron-star mergers can produce both gravitational waves and light, and that they are sites of heavy-element production in the Universe. As part of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, she shared in the 2017 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics.
At UTAS, Dr Siellez is developing a research, teaching and engagement program centred on southern-hemisphere transient astronomy. Her work aims to strengthen the role of Tasmanian optical facilities in rapid follow-up of gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae and gravitational-wave counterparts, while creating student pathways into real astronomical research. She is involved in national and international initiatives linked to SVOM, Rubin Observatory/LSST, OzGrav, robotic telescope networks and time-domain astronomy.
Dr Siellez is also a committed science communicator who connects physics with storytelling, music, visual art and public engagement. She has delivered public talks and outreach activities across Australia, France, French Polynesia and the United States, including schools, festivals, public lectures and interdisciplinary science-art events. Her engagement work includes gravitational-wave sonification, astronomy-inspired painting, dark-sky advocacy, and public programs highlighting the scientific, cultural and environmental importance of Tasmania’s skies.

Research fields: General relativity and gravitational waves, High energy astrophysics and galactic cosmic rays, Cosmology and extragalactic astronomy, Astronomical instrumentation, Astronomical sciences, Physical sciences

Supervisor: Doctor Ke Liu

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Ke Liu has established an internationally recognised research profile in climate adaptation science and agricultural systems modelling. His work has significantly advanced the representation of soil waterlogging stress in many farming systems models, repositioning waterlogging from a historically under-represented agronomic constraint to a quantifiable and scenario-testable climate risk within mainstream process-based crop modelling frameworks. He led the development and implementation of generic waterlogging algorithms within internationally recognised modelling platforms (APSIM Classic/Next Generation, DSSAT and SWAGMAN Destiny), enabling cross-regional and scenario-based risk quantification. These tools have been adopted within collaborative modelling programs and decision-support frameworks used in more than 30 countries, supporting improved assessment of soil waterlogging stress in climate impact analyses.
His 2023 Nature Communications paper, “Silver lining to a climate crisis in multiple prospects for alleviating crop waterlogging under future climates,” provided the first global-scale quantification of current and future waterlogging risk and mitigation potential and has helped catalyse broader research attention to waterlogging risk in climate impact assessments. This paper was featured by the journal under its Earth and Environmental Sciences Highlights and has been cited over 250 times and recognised as a Highly Cited Paper in the Web of Science. In recognition of the study’s significant impact, Dr. Liu was invited by the Nature editorial team to create a popular science video in 2024. The video has garnered more than 15,000 views on YouTube, reflecting the broad interest and influence of his research within the scientific community.
Dr Liu has also been invited to co-lead the AgMIP waterlogging initiative, a leading international platform dedicated to harmonising soil waterlogging stress representation across crop models. This collaboration culminated in a Nature Food review, “Gaps and strategies for accurate simulation of waterlogging impacts on crop productivity”, published in 2025, which identified key knowledge gaps and strategic pathways for advancing waterlogging simulation and modelling standards internationally, further advancing the global understanding and modeling of waterlogging effects on agricultural systems.
Since 2019, Dr Liu has published more than 110 refereed papers (35+ as first or corresponding author), ranked the 5th among the top 500 authors at the University of Tasmania (2022–2025) by scholarly output, with 4, 200+ citations and H-index of 37, Stanford/Elsevier's Top 2% Scientist Rankings (2025). Most of the papers published in prestigious journals such as Nature Food (2026, 2025, 2024) and Nature Communications (2026, 2023). These high-impact contributions reflect Dr. Liu’s strong commitment to research excellence, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and real-world impact, solidifying his reputation as a thought leader in the field of sustainable agriculture.

Bio: Dr Kyra Wood is an experienced academic and research project manager with a professional background in architecture and design. Her current research focusses on timber design and products at the University of Tasmania’s Centre for Sustainable Architecture with Wood. She works regularly with partners in the Australian timber and construction industries as well as several interstate and overseas research institutions.Kyra supervises post-graduate students at the University of Tasmania and as an adjunct at the University of the Sunshine Coast and is passionate about supporting early career researchers and postgraduate students to thrive in their chosen fields of research.BiographyPrior to commencing work as a timber researcher, Kyra worked as a registered architect in Adelaide (not currently practicing). She completed a PhD in architecture at the University of South Australia in 2018 titled: ‘Collaborative urban design for stakeholder engagement in world cultural heritage conservation: a practical study in the context of the citadel wall in Hue, Vietnam’. She is highly experienced in and dedicated to bringing together diverse groups of stakeholders to collaborate on complex or ‘wicked’ problems in relation to sustainable building and urban development challenges, having coordinated projects in multiple contexts including in Australia, Japan, South Korea and Vietnam. Although her research focus is currently on timber design and products, she maintains an ongoing interest in critical design ethnography and applies her background experience in collaborative design engagement in cross-cultural contexts to her current role managing various research projects that straddle the needs of the timber and design communities, where similarly complex challenges and diverse stakeholder groups exist.Kyra joined the Centre for Sustainable Architecture with Wood in 2018, and was quickly recruited as the principal researcher and team leader for two Launceston-based National Institute for Forest Products Innovation (NIFPI) projects focusing on timber durability. These pilot NIFPI projects were jointly funded by the Federal Government, state governments and industry to support small-scale, short-term collaborative research, and in 2022, the Australian Federal Government committed a further $100 million to a major Australian Forest and Wood Innovations (AFWI) program in Australia for ongoing research over the next 4-5 years that directly builds on the successes of three pilot NIFPI centres – in Launceston, Mount Gambier and Gippsland.In 2022, Kyra was nominated and selected as the inaugural Australian Ambassador for Women in Wood Science by the International Society of Wood Science and Technology (SWST) and joined the regional research collaboration program (RRC) as a Research Fellow, before a period of parental leave in 2023. She returned in 2024 to work on the development of a new AFWI centre application on supporting the timber industry's appearance products sector during the transition to an increased reliance on plantation and other younger hardwood resources. Kyra is currently chief investigator and project manager for this project titled: Supporting industry resilience in resource transition.

Bio: Dr Lieke Scheepers is a Research Fellow in the Environmental and Respiratory Health group at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research, University of Tasmania. She is an epidemiologist specialising in how early‑life environmental exposures influence health and development from pregnancy through to childhood and later life.

Her research focuses on a range of environmental exposures, including ambient air pollution, wildfire smoke, greenness, and pesticide exposure. Using a life‑course epidemiology approach, her work examines how these exposures affect pregnancy outcomes, birth, and long‑term health trajectories. Her research draws on large cohort studies and data linkage to generate robust evidence grounded in real‑world health outcomes, to inform prevention strategies and public‑health policy.

Dr Scheepers is the Lead of the Early‑Life Follow‑up (ELF) Stream of the Hazelwood Health Study, where she investigates the long-term cardiorespiratory, health and development of children exposed to a severe pollution event associated with a coal mine fire during their first 1000 days of life. She also provides scientific and operational leadership for the Statins Against Bushfire Smoke (SABS) clinical trial, which is testing whether interventions can reduce the cardiovascular impacts of wildfire smoke exposure.
She is always interested in hearing from motivated Honours and PhD students who would like to work on environmental exposures and early‑life health using large population datasets.

Bio: Luca is a marine geoscientist. He completed a Bachelor of Geological Sciences at the Università degli Studi di Pavia, followed by a Master of Geology and Land Management at Alma Mater Studiorum – Università di Bologna. He obtained his PhD from the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) at the University of Tasmania, where his research investigated the post-emplacement rifting of oceanic Large Igneous Provinces.

He subsequently joined IMAS as a Research Associate, where he focuses on marine and Antarctic geophysics.

Luca's research interests focus predominantly on marine geophysics, plate tectonics, ocean basin evolution, scientific ocean drilling, geodynamics, and sedimentology. His work integrates geological observations, marine geophysical data, and numerical modelling to investigate the processes that control lithospheric deformation and breakup, and the evolution of ocean basins.

He has participated in several oceanographic expeditions, including IODP Expedition 402 (Tyrrhenian Continent-Ocean Transition) aboard the JOIDES Resolution in the Mediterranean Sea, as well as research voyages on RV Investigator and RV Falkor in the Southern Ocean, Southwest Pacific, and Coral Sea.

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr McCallum is an expert in the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique. 'In VLBI we use signals from far distant radio galaxies to measure the Earth. In more detail, VLBI is used to measure the Earth's shape, the rotation of the Earth, polar motion, plate tectonics and the variation of these effects.'Dr. McCallum is the project scientist in the AuScope VLBI project, a research collaboration with Geoscience Australia, as part of the Positioning Australia project. She uses the university's own radio telescopes at Mt. Pleasant, the Northern Territory and in Western Australia, in common measurements together with telescopes all over the world. The goals of the VLBI group at UTAS are to guarantee best possible performance of our telescopes in global observations and to develop new methods to implement the next generation VLBI global observing system (VGOS). VGOS will be able to measure global distances to the level of a few millimetres, a necessity for important scientific and societal questions in geosciences, as for example the prediction of sea level rise of a few mm per year.VLBI is a key technique for measuring the Terrestrial Reference Frame (TRF), the Earth’s most precise coordinate system. Dr McCallum’s research focuses in the field of space ties, meaning that she tries to connect the geodetic techniques of the Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS, GPS), Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) and VLBI directly via a single satellite platform. Essential for space ties is VLBI satellite tracking. VLBI observations to satellites is an exciting and new technique, and Dr McCallum is leading an ARC DECRA project in this area.CareerDr Lucia McCallum is a Geodesist at the School of Physical Science, working in the group of radio astronomy. Her field of research is the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique, using signals from far distant radio galaxies to measure the Earth. After finishing her PhD at the Technische Universität in Vienna (Austria), she joined UTAS as a post-doc in 2014.Dr McCallum is involved in the AuScope VLBI project, working with the University's own radio telescopes at Mt. Role: Doctor

Bio: I'm the Associate Head of School for Learning and Teaching in the School of Geography, Planning and Spatial Sciences. I lead a team of exceptional people who are experts in nature conservation, climate science, landscape restoration, measuring and monitoring the natural environment, and making planful decisions that enhance sustainability and life on land. Our team teach in exciting ways and want to bring opportunities to learners worldwide via Tasmania's landscapes as living laboratories, irrespective of whether this is online or here in Hobart.

I'm an abiotic physical geographer who works in commodities (agriculture, forestry, mineral resources, geotourism) and nature (geo)conservation. My work is applied to geoheritage conservation and environmental education and extension. My contributions have been instrumental in advancing understanding of geoconservation theory and practise, and the management of geodiversity. I deliver Australia's sole undergraduate and postgraduate units in geoheritage and geotourism, bridging the gap between outdoor recreation, production landscapes and protected areas conservation practice. I'm passionate about bringing the cummulative expertise of my industry and practitioner networks into the classroom, where I use virtual and Tasmanian landscape exploration and professional training to build confidence, workforce capability and geographic knowledge.

My research is all about geoconservation. I have built a team of geoconservation researchers and practitioners who use and develop Tools for Abiotic Research in Nature (TARN). We examine and protect the values of cultural landscapes, develop digital tools to support geoconservation protections in UNESCO Global Geoparks, and examine degradation risks from natural hazards to geodiversity and geoheritage in protected areas. The tools that we create are sometimes instruments or new technologies, and sometimes they are decision-support frameworks or new processes for people managing soils, waterways, landforms and heritage places. I have managerial and/or leadership expertise in industry, government and academia. My strengths are in the coordination of large, inter-disciplinary teams, change management, advocacy, strategy, and managing for diversity. I think it takes many different types of people to solve problems, and I encourage my teams to contribute their diverse talents alongside industry and community. There are collaborative approaches to solve problems that balance the needs of humans and nature, and I like to bring people together to make this happen.

Supervisor: Doctor Nicholas Hookway

Role: Doctor

School: School of Social Sciences

Sub-organisation: Inveresk Campus

Bio: Dr Nicholas Hookway – sometimes known as the ‘happy sociologist’ – is Senior Lecturer in Sociology in the School of Social Sciences. Nick is a cultural sociologist whose research focuses on how social bonds, emotions and identity are being transformed by wider social change. He is internationally known for his research on kindness, everyday morality, sports charity, loneliness and digital methods. From Toyota to Cancer Council Tasmania, Nick’s research has led to successful partnerships with a range of local and national organisations. Nick has published in the best sociology journals in the world, including Sociology, British Journal of Sociology, The Sociological Review and Qualitative Research. His monograph Everyday Moralities: Doing it Ourselves in an Age of Uncertainty was awarded the prestigious Stephen Crook Memorial Prize (2020) for best book in Australian sociology. Nick is a leader in developing digital methods in sociology. His article on using blogs in social research has been cited over 1000 times. Nick was an elected member of The Australian Sociology Association (TASA) Executive Committee (Public Engagement Portfolio Leader) (2016–2020) and prior to this was the Co-Convenor of the Cultural Sociology TASA Thematic Group (2014–2016). He is currently an Associate Editor for the Journal of Sociology and serves on the Editorial Board of The Sociological Review, one of the world’s foremost sociology journals. Prior to this, he was an associate editor for Sociology, considered one of the world's best sociology journals. Nick is passionate about bringing sociological ideas to wider audiences. His research is regularly featured in local and national media outlets, including ABC Radio National, The Age, The Herald Sun and The New Daily. Nick was awarded the UTAS Vice-Chancellor’s Award for Outstanding Community Engagement (2016). Nick is currently the Graduate Research Coordinator for Sociology/Criminology, the School of Social Science Academic Lead for campus transition and is a member of the Northern Tasmanian Headspace Board. Outside work, Nick is a qualified tennis coach, average guitar player and Hawthorn Football Club and Roger Federer obsessive. Nick is current secretary of the Trevallyn Tennis Club and is a competitive runner and tennis player. He is the proud Dad of four: two young humans and two fur babies – Douggie the Dachshund and Cocoa the Tenterfield Terrier!

Research fields: Sociological methodology and research methods, Sociology, Human society

Bio: Peter is a Lecturer in the School of Architecture & Design at the University of Tasmania, specialising in computational design, digital fabrication, and sustainable material-driven approaches to architectural innovation. As an Early Career Researcher (ECR), his research investigates how emerging digital workflows can more effectively integrate material behaviour, fabrication constraints, and sustainability principles to advance architectural practice and regional manufacturing capacity. His work particularly emphasises the potential of latent wood-based materials within digitally integrated design and manufactured workflows.

Peter has more than two decades of combined professional and academic experience within the field of architecture. Since registering as an architect in 2005, he has worked across Tasmania, Melbourne, and London in roles that include Project Architect on residential, commercial, heritage, healthcare, and educational projects. In 2012, he co‑founded Pulp Studio Architecture, where he continues to serve as Director, contributing design leadership and technical expertise to residential and small‑scale commercial work.

His academic qualifications include a Bachelor of Environmental Design and Bachelor of Architecture from the University of Tasmania, a Master of Advanced Architecture (Digital Tectonics) from the Institute for Advanced Architecture of Catalonia in Barcelona, and a PhD in Architecture from the University of Technology Sydney. His doctoral work aligned with the Transformative Technologies & Data Poetics research group and examined computationally integrated approaches to non‑standardised plantation hardwood.

Bio: Dr Rachel Climie is an NHMRC Emerging Leader, Heart Foundation Future Leader Fellow and Clinical Exercise Physiologist. Rachel's research is focused on primordial prevention (the prevention of risk factor onset) of cardiovascular disease, commencing in early life. Rachel and her team are developing ways to identify young people at risk of premature heart disease and working with local communities to develop solutions to minimise this risk. Rachel completed her PhD at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research in 2016. She then undertook 2 years postdoctoral research studying cardiovascular epidemiology and arterial mechanics at Paris Research Center Cardiovasculaire (PARCC), France, where she is an Honorary Fellow. Rachel was awarded a Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship (and Paul Korner Award) to work with the Sports Cardiology research team at the Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute, before returning to Tasmania in 2021.
Rachel established and leads the Youth Vascular Consortium, a large international Consortium to investigate blood vessel ageing (vascular ageing) in young people. She is the co-lead a European network "Primordial Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and beyond in Europe"; Chair of the Knowledge Exchange Working Group on the European Artery Society/VascAgeNet, Chair of Advocacy and Society Liaison on the Hypertension Australia Board and on the Public Health Association of Australia Tasmanian Branch Committee. Rachel is a past member of the Australian Cardiovascular Alliance Emerging Leaders Committee and past HBPRCA ECR Committee Chair.

Rachel was awarded a Victorian Young Tall Poppy award in 2020 in recognition of her research.

Supervisor: Doctor Ruth Sharples

Role: Doctor

Bio: I am a marine scientist specialising in fisheries assessment, population ecology, and spatial data analysis. My current work at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS), University of Tasmania, focuses on assessing the status of key Tasmanian fisheries—including scalefish, Southern Calamari, and Pale Octopus—using analytical, model-based, and empirical approaches to evaluate stock trends, fishing pressure, and sustainability. I routinely provide science-based advice to government and industry through technical reports, working groups, and briefings.

My expertise spans stock assessment methods including CPUE standardization, surplus production models (CMSY, BSM, OCOM), and statistical modelling using GAMs and GLMs. I am highly proficient in R programming for data analysis and visualization, and experienced with GIS platforms (ArcGIS, QGIS) for spatial analysis of marine populations and fisheries.

My earlier career centered on marine vertebrate ecology, particularly the movements, habitat use, and population dynamics of seals and seabirds in relation to offshore energy infrastructure. This research, developed through positions at world-class institutions including the Sea Mammal Research Unit (University of St Andrews), CSIRO Oceans and Atmosphere, and IMAS, provides a strong foundation for understanding fish population dynamics within broader ecosystem contexts. Across academic, government, and consultancy roles, I have developed broad expertise in species distribution modelling, satellite telemetry, and the integration of ecological and human-use datasets.

I am committed to producing clear, defensible science that supports evidence-based management of marine resources and contributes to improved understanding of marine ecosystems.

Supervisor: Doctor Ryan Day

Role: Doctor

Bio: Ryan Day is Senior Research Fellow in Marine Animal Physiology and Biochemistry at University of Tasmania’s Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. In 2003, he received a Bachelor of Arts - Biology from the University of Chicago. In 2006, he received a Bachelor of Science - Marine Biology from the University of Queensland and in 2012, he received his PhD in Zoology from the University of Queensland.

Ryan has been a researcher at IMAS since 2012. One of his primary research areas are in measuring the impact of seismic surveys on marine invertebrates. In this field, his research has used quantification of acid-base physiology, haemolymph electrolyte and mineral homeostasis, immune function and oxidative stress to assess the health status of marine invertebrates including lobster, scallops and octopus to evaluate the impact of exposure to seismic air gun signals. The outcomes of this research have been incorporated by the federal regulatory body (NOPSEMA) for impact assessments to minimise harm to marine life.

In his second primary research area, Ryan investigates approaches for improving invertebrate fishery practices and outcomes, with a current focus on the commercial scallop. This research developed in response to reports of large-scale mortalities within the scallop fishery. In conducting an assessment of haemolymph physiology, including biochemistry and immune function, his research aims to identify environmental stressors underlying mortality to provide fishery management with options for responding to bed die offs. In similar work with the Southern Rock Lobster fishery response, Ryan authored an industry best practices guide with recommendations on handling and water quality management. Implementation of these recommendations has been attributed to eliminating mass mortality events and halving mortality rates by industry partners. This work has recently been extended to the fishing vessel component of the industry and projects to apply this research to other marine invertebrate fisheries are in development. In addition to his recent work with invertebrates, Ryan’s PhD research focused on digestive physiology in marine fishes, in which he characterised digestive strategies in fishes that lack a stomach.

Research fields: Animal structure and function, Aquaculture and fisheries stock assessment, Invertebrate biology, Zoology, Biological sciences, Fisheries sciences, Agricultural, veterinary and food sciences

Role: Doctor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: School of Natural Sciences — Chemistry

Bio: Dr Santosh Kisan Pagire is a Research Fellow at the University of Tasmania (Australia), working with Prof. Alex C. Bissember on multiple ARC-funded programs in light-driven catalysis. He also serves as Assistant Professor of Chemistry at Indian Institute of Technology, Banaras Hindu University (IIT–BHU), Varanasi (India).

Born in Maharashtra (India), Santosh’s academic trajectory transformed early in his BSc when disciplined mentorship from Prof. Dilip R. Thube and Prof. Tukaram S. Thopate ignited his passion for synthetic organic chemistry, particularly for organic reaction mechanisms. Rising from a below-average student to one of the top three in his class at the New Arts, Commerce, and Science College, Parner, he also ranked 5th in Chemistry across all colleges under the University of Pune in 2009.

During his Master’s degree at the Department of Chemistry, University of Pune (2009–2011), he received the Eklavya (merit) and Kawathekar (need-cum-merit) fellowships. In 2010, he qualified the MH-SET (Maharashtra State Eligibility Test) on his first attempt, and in 2011, he secured a highly competitive All-India Rank of 22 (top 1%) in the CSIR–NET examination—again on the first attempt. He trained under distinguished teachers, including Prof. Murzban S. Wadia, Prof. Mukund G. Kulkarni, and Prof. Shridhar R. Gadre, with exceptional mentorship from Prof. Dilip D. Dhavale FASc (Head and Distinguished Professor, Department of Chemistry, University of Pune).

Immediately after his Master’s in 2011, Santosh dedicated a few months to teaching chemistry free of charge to rural students at Dhokeshwar Mahavidyalaya in Maharashtra (Affil. University of Pune)—an experience that strengthened his communication, empathy, and commitment to accessible science education.

In 2011–2013, he undertook early research training in asymmetric organocatalysis, international metal catalysis work with Prof. Pher G. Andersson (Sweden) and Prof. Thavendran Govender (South Africa), and advanced total-synthesis training at NCL Pune (India) with Dr Subhash P. Chavan. This broad foundation led to multiple international PhD offers, independent of fellowship outcomes.

In 2013, he secured the prestigious DAAD Fellowship—on his first attempt—to pursue a PhD in Synthetic Organic Chemistry at the University of Regensburg (Germany) under Prof. Oliver Reiser, completing his doctorate in December 2017.
Following his PhD, Santosh obtained the postdoctoral positions he most aspired to, and once again the associated elite international fellowships were awarded to his research proposals on the first attempt. His postdoctoral research included:• DFG Walter Benjamin Postdoctoral Fellow, BIKAKEN (Affil. The University of Tokyo, Japan) with Profs. Masakatsu Shibasaki and Naoya Kumagai (2018–2021);• Marie Skłodowska–Curie Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Bristol—ranked #1 in the UK for Chemistry (REF 2021)—with Prof. Varinder K. Aggarwal FRS (2021–2023);• followed by a research stay with Prof. Lutz Ackermann, University of Göttingen, Germany (2023–2024).

In 2024–2025, he transitioned to industry, leading a Discovery Chemistry group at Syngene International Ltd., India, for Kestrel Therapeutics (USA), contributing to early-stage drug discovery. In March 2025, he joined Chanakya University, where his clear, application-focused teaching approach transformed initially uninterested BTech engineering students into highly engaged learners—earning him the highest teaching feedback ratings across the cohort. He moved to the University of Tasmania (Australia) in September 2025 to resume his research journey.

Santosh’s research integrates visible- and near-infrared (NIR) photocatalysis, radical chemistry, asymmetric synthesis, and phosphorus chemistry to develop selective and sustainable molecular transformations. He has published in leading journals, including Accounts of Chemical Research (IF ~24.6), Angewandte Chemie International Edition (16.8), Journal of the American Chemical Society (16.4), and ACS Catalysis (13.7), and has accumulated >3,300 citations, with a strong first-author record in top-tier Q1 journals.

Research fields: Organic chemical synthesis, Photochemistry, Organometallic chemistry, Organic chemistry, Chemical sciences, Physical chemistry, Inorganic chemistry
