Bio: Associate Professor Cynthia Honan is an APHRA endorsed senior practising clinical neuropsychologist with specialist clinical training in neuropsychological assessment and cognitive rehabilitation. Cynthia's areas of research focus largely on Moderate-to-Severe Traumatic Brain Injury and Multiple Sclerosis and the cognitive and psychological changes that result from these disorders. She has a specific interest in social cognition, cognitive fatigue and cognitive biomarkers, meta-social-cognitive functioning, and functional outcomes (e.g., employment and meaningful occupation). Cynthia recently led a large national project to develop clinical practice guidelines for the management of psychosocial difficulties (relating to mental health, behaviour, and social cognition) in moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, and is now part of a national team to implement these guidelines into clinical practice.BiographyBefore joining the University of Tasmania, Cynthia was a postdoctoral research fellow and lecturer at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) from 2012 to 2015. Supervisor: Associate Professor Emily Ogier

Role: Associate Professor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Bio: I’m a marine social researcher, and I apply my research skills to support marine and coastal communities and sectors in sustainable transitions.I work with marine ecologists, fish stock scientists, resource economists, biogeochemists, climate modellers, political scientists and others to integrate knowledge and explore solutions.I coordinate research programs concerned with human dimensions of marine systems. 'Human dimensions' refers to communities, economies, behaviours, institutions, markets, knowledge production, other collective actions which interact with these marine systems. I partner with fisheries and aquaculture communities and sectors, inclusive of Indigenous, commercial and recreational organisations and leaders. I design and share socio-economic and socio-ecological assessments to support public policy development and adaptive management of fisheries and aquaculture sectors domestically. More and more I work on future-facing research to support ocean leaders and communities anticipate and govern change. My research helps explore opportunities for socially responsible climate action in response to rapidly warming oceans.

Supervisor: Associate Professor Erin Roehrer

Role: Associate Professor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: Information and Communication Technology

Bio: Associate Professor Erin Roehrer is a member of the School of Information and Communication Technology at the University of Tasmania. She is a leader in designing, delivering, and advancing technology‑enhanced learning that supports diverse learners and drives innovation across transnational education contexts.

A Fellow of the Higher Education Academy, Erin brings a collaborative and reflective teaching philosophy that empowers both students and colleagues. She has led major curriculum renewals, received multiple learning and teaching awards, and serves as Associate Editor for Australia’s highest‑impact education journal, the Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. Erin is a values‑driven academic leader who embodies a “leading from within and alongside” philosophy in every role. She has held a range of leadership positions and is currently Deputy Chair of Academic Senate, Chair of the Curriculum Quality Assurance Committee (CQAC), and Associate Head Students (School of ICT). In these roles, Erin shapes inclusive student experiences, supports staff development, and champions academic excellence through collaborative, context‑aware leadership across local, national, and international partnerships.

embedding_items.title: Associate Professor Hossein Enshaei
embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Hossein Enshaei

Role: Associate Professor

School: Australian Maritime College

Sub-organisation: Seafaring and Maritime Operations

Bio: Dr Hossein Enshaei interest is in the field of marine technologies.Hossein commenced his career as a seafarer and has 13 years of service as a navigator on ocean going vessels. He left the sea in 1999 while he was a Master mariner to join the training institute to train seafarer and served as a lecturer and head of deck department. Upon his graduation as a naval architect in 2004, he joined shipbuilding industry and completed three unique projects. Hossein pursued his career as a maritime researcher at Newcastle University in UK while completing his PhD and served as a researcher over several national, regional and international projects while contributing to the teaching of undergraduate and postgraduate engineering programs. Since joining Australian Maritime College (AMC) in 2014, Hossein actively engaged in multidisciplinary research focusing on ship operations, developing advanced modelling, control and optimisation algorithms, and applying them to study ship’s stability and shipboard powering systems. He collaborates with individuals from different hierarchical levels and disciplines within and outside the university to enhance areas of research excellence and attract the best students and researchers

embedding_items.text:
algorithms, and applying them to study ship’s stability and shipboard powering systems. He collaborates with individuals from different hierarchical levels and disciplines within and outside the university to enhance areas of research excellence and attract the best students and researchers from around the world. Hossein established and led a unique Real-Time Power Systems Simulator (RTPSS) facility in AMC for designing digital-twin for existing and future marine vehicles and autonomous AUVs. RTPSS not only complements existing internationally recognised AMC hydrodynamics, fluid mechanics and AUV facilities, but adds a state-of-the-art sovereign capability to Australian Maritime industry. Hossein's research interests are in ship's dynamic stability and marine informatics. He performs advanced research on ship systems, and develops decision making tools using mathematical modelling, simulation and optimisation techniques.

His technical leadership and specialist skills in this space are set to drive the advancement and modernisation of these modules, which are currently utilised as part of undergraduate training in most Schools of Medicine, Pharmacy, and Dentistry in Australia.He has also developed a novel 3D learning experience (https://www.pharmacysim.com) which helps to prepare students to go out into the workforce and face real-life situations. embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Ivona Mladineo

Role: Associate Professor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Bio: Associate Professor Ivona Mladineo is an internationally recognised aquatic animal health and parasitology researcher whose work focuses on fish and invertebrate diseases, host–parasite interactions, and health management in aquaculture. She has made significant contributions to understanding marine parasites, particularly zoonotic nematodes such as Anisakis, and the impacts of pathogens on fish health, aquaculture sustainability, and food safety. Her research spans parasitology, disease ecology, functional biology, and the development of innovative approaches to aquatic animal health and disease control. With an extensive publication record and a strong international research profile, Ivona has led and contributed to numerous multidisciplinary projects addressing emerging challenges in aquaculture, climate change, aquatic biosecurity, and pathogen management. She currently serves as Associate Professor in Aquatic Animal Health at the University of Tasmania and continues to collaborate widely with academic, government, and industry partners to advance sustainable aquatic animal production and ecosystem health.

Research fields: Fish pests and diseases, Host-parasite interactions, Innate immunity, Proteins and peptides, Microbiology, Fisheries sciences, Agricultural, veterinary and food sciences, Evolutionary

Role: Associate Professor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Oceans and Cryosphere

Bio: Dr Jacqueline Halpin is geologist and Associate Professor at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS). Her research mainly examines dynamic processes occurring in the Earth's crust, including: crustal growth and architecture; continental rifting, breakup and exhumation; and tectonic cycles and supercontinent configurations. Jacqueline is currently working on Antarctic geoscience themes including past ice sheet change and Earth-cryosphere interactions, as part of the ARC Australian Centre for Excellence in Antarctic Science Special Research Initiative (ACEAS).Jacqueline joined IMAS in 2015. She completed her science undergraduate degree with Honours in Geology from the University of Melbourne in 2001, and was awarded her PhD, on the tectonic evolution of the Rayner Complex in East Antarctica, from the University of Sydney in 2007. She has also worked for the Centre of Ore Deposit and Earth Sciences (CODES) as a research fellow and at Macquarie University (2007-2015) and University of Sydney (2011-2012) as a lecturer and research associate.

School: Wicking Dementia Research Education Centre

Bio: Dr Jenna Ziebell is an Associate Professor in the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. Her research interests include the role of microglia (the brain's immune cells) in health, ageing and disease; understanding traumatic brain injury and health education. Dr Ziebell has a strong interest in how the brain's immune system is altered, or primed, with ageing or injury and how this may lead to neurological diseases such as dementia.Dr Ziebell has a long-standing interest in the role of inflammation in neurological diseases, particularly the role of microglia. She is a mid-career researcher who established the Microglia and Neurological Diseases Laboratory at the University of Tasmania. Prior to this Jenna co-established the Translational Neurotrauma Program in Phoenix, AZ, USA; where she led a research team that investigated the role of microglia in acute neurological diseases. Her interest in the role of microglia in health and disease was ignited during her PhD at Monash University and has continued throughout postdoctoral research at the University of Adelaide (2009-2011), University of Kentucky

Dr Ziebell’s areas of interest include microglial activation in health and disease, trauma and injury related circuitry rearrangements, microglial priming and senescence in ageing and dementia; and more recently the social impact of intimate partner violence.

Bio: Kate Booth is a human geographer and activist academic. Her work addresses socio-ecological inequity in the context of rapid and unprecedented global change.She leads the Just Collapse platform - addressing global collapse with a commitment to socio-ecological theory, equitable change, and emancipatory politics. This platform mixes academic research, education, and activism, and leverages Kate's research investigating geographies of insurance and society in a changing climate. About her new book, In Collapse: When Insurance and Climate Collide - "In Collapse unsettles. Booth forces us to turn and face, head-on, the many discomfiting truths about living in and with climate breakdown. But it also clarifies and empowers. With their critical interrogation of collapse through the prism of insurance, we better know what worlds may be ending, which already have, and how to look for solidarity amidst the wreckage. Bio: I am the Alex Gadomski Fellow. I lead a small team working on the immunology and genetics underpinning Bone Marrow Failure and haematopoiesis within the School of Medicine. I also teach into first, second and third year research methodology, molecular biology and biochemistry subjects in the College of Health and Medicine. My research work focusses on using molecular biology techniques such as single-cell sequencing and CRISPR to understand more about the development of blood cells, and to generate new potential therapeutics.BiographyI have always been interested in the mechanisms that underpin the way that cells are generated to make up the blood, and how the body makes sure we have the right number of cells to carry oxygen, fight infection and clot the blood where there is an injury. I have studied this topic in some amazing places to research, in Melbourne at the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, where my PhD was focused on the generation and specification of antibody secreting cells. From WEHI I moved to Cambridge (UK) to work at the Babraham Institute of Medical Research, where my postdoctoral studies investigated the role of RNA-binding proteins in

From WEHI I moved to Cambridge (UK) to work at the Babraham Institute of Medical Research, where my postdoctoral studies investigated the role of RNA-binding proteins in B cell development. I returned to Australia to work at Monash University, and WEHI, continuing my work on the generation and specification of blood cells. I am delighted to be back home to Tasmania (I grew up in Launceston) working on understanding Bone Marrow Failure Syndrome, autoimmunity and haematopoiesis and trying to find new therapies and markers for these diseases. embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Mark Hinder

Role: Associate Professor

School: School of Psychological Sciences

Sub-organisation: Psychology

Bio: As people age, they experience changes in motor control (such as the coordination of their limbs as well as the dexterous control of hand and finger movements) and in their cognitive abilities (skills like decision-making, problem-solving, learning and memory).A/Prof Mark Hinder's research looks at how changes in the structure and functioning of the brain affect our ability to do these everyday motor and cognitive tasks. He examines how these changes are related to the fact that some older adults show more deterioration of these abilities while others retain a high level of motor and cognitive function late into senescence.As a motor neuroscientist, a focus of his research is to determine which areas of the brain are critically involved in the performance of everyday tasks and how these areas communicate with each other during various components of the task. He uses a technique known as transcranial magnetic stimulation (or TMS) to investigate the level of activation of different brain regions, and how different brain regions communicate, while participants perform tasks in the laboratory. By comparing the results from younger subjects, healthy older adults, and older people with mild cognitive impairment, he

embedding_items.title: Associate Professor Mark Hinder
embedding_items.text: investigate the level of activation of different brain regions, and how different brain regions communicate, while participants perform tasks in the laboratory. By comparing the results from younger subjects, healthy older adults, and older people with mild cognitive impairment, he evaluates how the different patterns of connections in the brain relate to how well people are able to do at different tasks.‘It seems that those people who maintain better functional connectivity between different brain regions show better function into older age,’ A/Prof Hinder says.With Australia’s population ageing rapidly, his results could be important to the development of interventions aimed at maintaining motor and cognitive function, or delaying the deleterious effects of cognitive decline. One aspect of his research is to look at the role changes in brain structure and function play in dementia and other age-related conditions where people experience accelerated declines in cognition or motor function. He is also examining how the brain compensates through a process known as plasticity, for example in response to declines in function caused by dementia or stroke.‘Essentially, we are asking: when there is damage to one area of the brain, is the brain able to compensate by recruiting other areas to maintain the ability to undertake certain tasks?’Ultimately, A/Prof Hinder’s research

There is already some evidence to suggest an association between brain stimulation and short-term improvements in performance.‘Our goal is to understand this better and see whether we can develop therapeutic protocols that lead to sustained improvements in performance.’In his research, A/Prof Hinder has collaborated with researchers at the School of Medicine, Menzies Institute for Medical Research and the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. ‘The University has great facilities for doing ageing-related research,’ A/Prof Hinder says. ‘One of the major benefits of working here is the ease with which you can establish collaborations with world-renowned researchers in their respective fields.’ His previous projects have involved collaborations with Trinity College Dublin as well as colleagues at University of Queensland and University of Western Australia. I’m endlessly surprised by the ideas students have”. embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Associate Professor Nicole Hill

Role: Associate Professor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Ecology and Biodiversity

Bio: Dr Nicole Hill a quantitative marine ecologist who leads a team of researchers focussing on mapping and predicting marine biodiversity. Dr Hill's team uses the latest techniques at the interface of ecology and statistics and her research has impact in the areas of conservation, spatial planning, fisheries, ecosystem assessment and the development of monitoring programs. A key component of her team's current research focusses understanding and mapping the current distribution of benthic and demersal ecosystems in the Southern Ocean and predicting how they may change in response to climate change and other pressures.A selection of her team’s research includes; mapping the circumpolar distribution of benthic biodiversity, developing an integrative index for Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems (VME) from imagery, understanding how environmental variability affects Patagonian Toothfish catch rates, assessing methods to detect ecological change, quantifying recent change in demersal fish and zooplankton assemblages and using these outputs to help optimize monitoring.

Research fields: Ecological impacts of climate change and ecological adaptation, Conservation and biodiversity, Climate change impacts and adaptation, Environmental sciences, Environmental management

She then joined the laboratory of Dr Adele Holloway where she sought to understand how leukaemic fusion proteins disrupt epigenetic mechanisms in Acute Myeloid Leukaemia.Phillippa undertook her post-doctoral research training in the laboratory of Professor Peter Jones at the University of Southern California, USA (2008-2011). Bio: Dr Taryn Noble is Associate Professor in Antarctic paleoclimatology at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. She is interested in understanding the ocean’s role in past climate change. Her research is focused on the interaction between the ocean and Antarctic Ice Sheet during periods of past climate warming; using geochemical approaches to reconstruct the semnsitivity of vulnerable marine-based glaciers in East Antarctica, and the implications of ice sheet change on biogeochemical processes in Southern Ocean.Taryn applies geochemical methods in seawater and marine sediment cores to reconstruct ocean circulation, sediment provenance and biological fluxes in the ocean. Paleoclimate records are useful because they can provide insight into processes and feedbacks in the climate system, which can aid the representation of physical processes in ice sheet and climate models.BiographyDr Taryn Noble moved to the University of Tasmania after earning her PhD at the University of Cambridge in Southern Ocean Paleoceanography. embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor Alyssa Marshell

Role: Doctor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Fisheries and Aquaculture

Bio: Dr Alyssa Marshell is a fisheries scientist with over 20 years of international experience in applied, interdisciplinary marine science research. Her research spans fields such as fish population dynamics, fisheries sustainability, and marine ecology across the Indo-Pacific, Indian Ocean, and around Australia.
After earning her BSc in Marine Biology from James Cook University, Alyssa began her career as a dive instructor and marine tour guide across the Great Barrier Reef, Red Sea, Madagascar, and the Mediterranean. She later completed an MSc in Guam and a PhD at the University of Queensland, before leading fisheries science projects in Palau as a Post-Doctoral Research Fellow, and in Oman as an Assistant Professor at Sultan Qaboos University. Her research blends tools such as BRUVs and ROV video surveys, acoustic telemetry, external tagging, and field surveys to address ecological and management challenges. Alyssa has deep cross-cultural international experience and a strong track record in managing complex research projects.

Andreas is an internationally recognized expert in marine biotoxins, harmful algal bloom management and seafood safety. He is a Senior Research Fellow in the Health Seafood research group at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. His research focuses on understanding key physiological and cellular processes in harmful microalgae and applying this knowledge to actively improve marine biotoxin risk management and biosecurity. He provides scientific advice to SafeFish, the National Seafood Safety and Market Access program and coordinates the Australian ciguatera poisoning working group. His research directly informs risk management practices to safeguard commercially important finfish, lobster and abalone fisheries.BiographyAndreas completed his PhD at the University of Tasmania in 2017, where he explored the use of clay minerals to successfully mitigate the impact of fish-killing algal blooms. Bio: The circulation of the Southern Ocean has an outsized role in global climate by controlling how heat makes its way towards the Antarctic continent and how much anthropogenic heat and carbon are stored away in the abyssal ocean. I use a suite of observational data to better understand the mechanisms for transporting heat across the Southern Ocean, where and how those warm waters get onto the Antarctic continental shelf, and what is responsible for changes in the deepest, densest waters in the ocean.

Bio: Anya is Senior Lecturer in Philosophy and Ethics in the School of Humanities, University of Tasmania. Interdisciplinary collaborations are at the core of Anya’s research interests. She investigates the intersections of phenomenology with philosophy of mind, the philosophy of perception, the philosophy of psychiatry, embodied and social cognition, enactivism, ethics, aesthetics and Buddhist Philosophy. Anya has received funding from national and international institutions to support her research projects and also to facilitate the dissemination of her own work and the work of others through publications, organising workshops and conferences. Notable among these was The Inhuman Gaze, a three-day multi-disciplinary international conference spanning the disciplines of philosophy, cognitive neuroscience, psychiatry, psychology, sociology and aesthetics, which was hosted in Paris 2018 - https://theinhumangaze.com/. Papers from this conference were published by Routledge in an edited volume for which she was the chief editor.

Bio: Ben has been working in Engineering Education for approximately 7 years, after completing his PhD in Electrical Engineering (power distribution optimisation). Ben’s research has generally been focused on the application of computer systems to solving problems in renewable power systems, which aligns well with the newly introduced “Climate Safe Engineering” focus of the school in both curriculum and research. Bio: Dr Bennet McComish is a Senior Research Fellow in the Menzies Institute for Medical Research at the University of Tasmania. He leads the Evolutionary Medicine group within the MS Research Flagship.Bennet's background is in molecular evolution and bioinformatics, and he currently leads a team investigating the evolutionary origins of genetic risk factors for multiple sclerosis. This work includes scanning human genome data for signatures of natural selection (including local adaptation) and modeling evolutionary processes such as admixture and genetic drift. He has worked across a range of complex diseases, including multiple sclerosis and inherited eye diseases. He manages a dedicated genomics high-performance computing cluster, supporting and training research staff and students who use the cluster. His work involves analysing genome sequence data using bioinformatic tools to identify the genetic variants that are most likely to be involved in causing disease.Bennet completed a PhD in Computational Biology in the Allan Wilson Centre for Molecular Ecology and Evolution (New Zealand). He joined the School of Mathematics and Physics at the University of Tasmania in 2013 as a postdoctoral researcher

Bio: Dr Brooklyn Fraser is a Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Research Fellow. Her research is focused on the health and fitness of Australian children, with a strong interest in the long-term cardiovascular health benefits of greater fitness.

Brooklyn completed a Bachelor of Biotechnology and Medical Research with First Class Honours in 2015. Brooklyn received her PhD from the University of Tasmania in 2019. Brooklyn’s PhD explored the association between childhood muscular fitness and type 2 diabetes related outcomes in adulthood. Her research helped identify muscular fitness, in childhood and across the life course, as a target to help prevent type 2 diabetes. Brooklyn was awarded the Menzies Institute for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship in 2020 and a nationally competitive Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship in 2022. Brooklyn’s postdoctoral research examines the health and fitness of Australian children, with a strong focus on the long-term cardiovascular health benefits of greater fitness.

Brooklyn works with large observational studies with longitudinal data and is experienced with analytic techniques relevant to longitudinal data including life-course modelling. Brooklyn has independently developed highly engaged, impactful and ongoing international collaborations with leading paediatric exercise science experts, formalised within the Global Youth Fitness Consortium

Role: Doctor

School: School of Social Sciences

Bio: I am a Senior Lecturer in International Relations in the School of Social Sciences at the University of Tasmania. Prior to this, I was Senior Lecturer and Course Coordinator at the University of Sussex, and Associate Professor and Head of International Studies at the University of Nottingham Ningbo, China. I am author of the textbook 'World Politics. A Critical Introduction'.
My academic trajectory has been shaped by a cosmopolitan background: I have studied and worked in five countries, across two continents, and in three languages. This lived experience informs my commitment to critical approaches in International Relations. My research and teaching are driven by the conviction that decolonising, indigenising, and feminising the discipline are not only matters of justice but also of intellectual integrity. I seek to challenge dominant narratives in order to generate new ways of understanding global politics and our place within it.
In addition to my academic work, I maintain a broad range of interests, from kendo and kayaking to bushwalking and textile crafts, and I am also a mother of two.

Bio: Dr Charlotte Dunn is a Senior Lecturer in Classics in the School of Humanities and Social Science. Charlotte’s research areas include the Age of Alexander the Great and the Hellenistic Age, with a particular focus on the lives and careers of the Successors who rose to power after Alexander’s death to form empires of their own. One of the major subjects of Charlotte’s research is the colourful Demetrius ‘the Besieger’ Poliorcetes, and she co-authored the first full-length monograph on the life of this infamous Hellenistic king, Demetrius the Besieger (2020).Her research expertise also includes the use of political imagery and propaganda in the Ancient World, the development of the Hellenistic royal dynasties and their family dynamics, historiography, medical humanities, as well as the field of numismatics.BiographyBefore joining the University of Tasmania, Charlotte studied at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand where she completed her undergraduate and postgraduate degrees, in Classics, Greek and Latin. Bio: Dr Claire Eccleston is a Senior Lecturer in Dementia Care in the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. She has a keen interest in dementia education and literacy, and in health literacy and how it can be supported by health workers. She brings experience in quantitative and mixed methods research relating to the assessment of knowledge, attitudes, and health literacy about dementia and dementia risk reduction. She has developed and validated a number of related survey instruments, and has supported their translation into many different languages. She has a breadth of experience in evaluating the effectiveness of education across multiple modes such as massive open online courses, online undergraduate courses, training of health and care professionals, and clinical placements. BiographyDr Eccleston has a PhD in quantitative ecology from Griffith University, Queensland. After returning to Tasmania, she worked part time as a Research Fellow on the Wicking Teaching Aged Care Facilities Program from 2011 to 2015, leading the evaluation component of the second part of this program between 2013-2015. The program aimed to prototype Teaching Aged Care Facilities by providing healthcare students with a quality clinical placement in residential aged care. Dr

In 2017, Claire led an investigation of dementia knowledge and education needs in the Tasmanian community and since then has been a member of teams investigating the attitudes, experiences and knowledge needs of the current and future health and care workforce. She is currently an investigator on multiple projects such as a major project to increase awareness of traumatic brain injury and the ISLAND project which aims to understand how we can promote behavioural change to reduce risk of dementia, as well as a project exploring health literacy responsiveness in the University's health and care students.Qualifications

Bio: Damien Kingston is a Hobart-born guitarist, composer, researcher, and educator whose practice spans performance, recording, curriculum leadership, and community engagement across jazz, improvised music, and contemporary creative practice. After completing a Bachelor of Music at the University of Tasmania, Damien relocated to Europe, working as a freelance musician and completing a Masters of Music at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam (2013) under Dutch guitar luminaries Martijn van Iterson and Jesse van Ruller, following an active period in Berlin's jazz and improvised music community.

Returning to Tasmania, Damien completed a PhD at the University of Tasmania (2018) and joined the Conservatorium as a casual lecturer in 2014 before moving to ongoing employment in 2019. He currently holds three formal leadership positions - Associate Head Learning and Teaching, Course Coordinator, and Honours Coordinator - with accountability for the Bachelor of Music, Diploma of Music, Associate Degree, and Honours award courses. His teaching philosophy integrates academic rigour, industry authenticity, and inclusive practice, supporting students from diverse backgrounds to develop professional skills and discover their own artistic voice.

embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor David Green

Role: Doctor

Bio: David is a marine spatial ecologist and Lecturer in Marine Spatial Ecology at IMAS (Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies), University of Tasmania. With around 15 years of experience in biologging and animal tracking, he has worked across more than 15 marine predator species, spanning temperate, Subantarctic and Antarctic systems. His research combines biotelemetry, statistical and mechanistic modelling approaches to resolve links between the physical environment and ecological processes across multiple trophic levels, from oceanographic drivers through mid trophic prey dynamics to top predator foraging ecology. He holds a PhD from IMAS, a strong publication record built over more than a decade, and extensive field leadership experience, including coordinating tagging voyages and expeditions across remote and polar systems. His work increasingly bridges research and policy, contributing to international spatial conservation and management processes, alongside a growing teaching, supervision, and mentorship portfolio.

Research fields: Marine and estuarine ecology (incl. marine ichthyology), Infectious agents, Community ecology (excl. invasive species ecology), Ecology, Biological sciences, Microbiology

embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor Elly Quinlan

Role: Doctor

Bio: I'm a psychologist (clinical, educational & developmental), senior lecturer, and supervisor with a focus on professional training, ethics, and inclusive practice. I've contributed to the development and review of postgraduate psychology programs across several institutions. I teach into postgraduate psychology, supervise both research and clinical placements, and support students as they navigate the realities of becoming a psychologist. I particularly value working closely with students as they develop their professional identity and confidence.
My research focuses on strengthening the structures and supports that shape postgraduate psychology training and professional practice. I've explored areas such as practicum logbooks, sexual abuse inquiry, fostering tolerance of uncertainty, supporting students experiencing competency issues, and the development of mentoring programs. I also have research interests in neurodiversity and neurodivergence, role-play and gaming, recovery-oriented approaches, and the experiences of mental health carers.A consistent focus of my work is translating research into practical resources and guidance that can be used in training and professional settings.
Clinically, I have worked with young people experiencing trauma, attachment disruptions, grief and loss, sexual abuse, disability, and neurodivergence, and I am

Bio: Gabi Mocatta is a communication and journalism researcher who currently studies communicational responses to climate change. This multifocal work takes place at the site where climate change science, public understanding and collective discourse on climate change and environmental policy intersect. Gabi also examines media representations of climate change - given most people derive their understanding of our changing climate from the media. She additionally researches climate literacy, to better understand what spurs climate action at all levels of society. Gabi is currently Senior Research Fellow in Climate Science Communication with the globally-known Climate Futures Research Group in the School of Geography, Planning and Spatial Sciences.A former journalist, Gabi began her academic career at the University of Tasmania teaching journalism. She undertook her PhD in environmental communication at the university's Media School. Gabi then worked as Lecturer in Communication and Course Director of the Masters in Communication at Deakin University, Melbourne. She has been a member of the Climate Futures research group since 2020, bringing expertise in climate communication and climate science translation for public policy making and behaviour change. Climate Futures works with with a wide range of industry and government stakeholders to

Bio: Dr Gabriela Bodea is a Senior Lecturer in Biomedicine and Head of the Molecular Neurogenetics Lab at the Tasmanian School of Medicine, University of Tasmania.

Dr Bodea completed her PhD with the highest distinction, summa cum laude, at the University of Bonn (2014, Germany). Dr Bodea subsequently pursued postdoctoral training at the Mater Research Institute and then at the Queensland Brain Institute, University of Queensland, Australia. During this time, Dr Bodea's work significantly contributed to understanding the role of LINE-1 retrotransposons, a class of mobile DNA elements colloquially known as “jumping genes” in generating genetic diversity within neurons during mammalian neurodevelopment (Cell, 2015; Genome Research 2017, 2022, 2023; Nature Neuroscience, 2024). In mid-2025, Dr Bodea relocated to the University of Tasmania, assuming a teaching and research role and establishing the Molecular Neurogenetics Research Lab.

Dr Bodea's Molecular Neurogenetics (MNG) Research Lab investigates the mechanisms of neural plasticity, specifically how environmental exposures shape the genetic identity of neurons and direct

embedding_items.title: Doctor Gabriela Bodea
embedding_items.text:
of Tasmania, assuming a teaching and research role and establishing the Molecular Neurogenetics Research Lab.

Dr Bodea's Molecular Neurogenetics (MNG) Research Lab investigates the mechanisms of neural plasticity, specifically how environmental exposures shape the genetic identity of neurons and direct the formation of mammalian brain circuitry, enabling adaptive processes. The MNG team also aims to understand how environmental factors, immune signalling, and genetic predisposition contribute to complex neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative conditions, such as schizophrenia and Parkinson’s disease. To address these questions, the MNG team applies a powerful, integrated toolkit spanning cellular and molecular biology, neuroscience, and genomics. This multidisciplinary approach enables the MNG team to precisely dissect gene-regulatory mechanisms and delineate the cellular and molecular pathways that drive vulnerability and resilience in the central nervous system.

Our research has secured prestigious and highly competitive funding, including fellowships from the German Research Foundation (DFG, 2014-2016), the NHMRC-ARC Dementia Research Development (2016-2020), and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation (BBRF) Young Investigator Award (2025-2027). Bio: Dr. Gary Morris is a lecturer within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre. He completed his PhD in 2017 at the University of New South Wales, before undertaking postdoctoral research at University of Technology, Sydney, from 2017-2019.

In 2019, Dr. Morris joined the Perivascular Research Group at the University of Tasmania, led by Professor Brad Sutherland, as a Research Fellow. In 2025, Dr. Morris began his research group, the Gliovascular Research Group, within the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre at UTAS. His research investigates how non-neuronal cells residing within the brain, and around the vasculature of the brain, contribute to vascular functions including the control of brain blood flow, blood-brain-barrier protection and brain waste removal. embedding_items.title: Doctor Greg Walter
embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor Greg Walter

Role: Doctor

Bio: Greg is an evolutionary ecologist that seeks to answer fundamental questions in ecology and evolution that improve our understanding of how biodiversity is created, and how populations cope with novel environments. As a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Bristol (2017-2020), he tested mechanisms that promote persistence in novel environments by conducting large-scale field experiments in Sicily using seeds and clones of two species of Senecio wildflowers. For his DECRA fellowship at Monash University (2020-2024), he used laboratory experiments to identify the mechanisms that help populations to maintain ecological resilience in response to stressful environments representing climate change scenarios. His current research goals are to understand how plants evolve to buffer environmental variation that includes climate extremes and apply this knowledge to develop climate-resilient crops through collaboration with plant breeders and Indigenous communities.

Supervisor: Doctor Hannah Fair

Role: Doctor

School: Wicking Dementia Research Education Centre

Sub-organisation: Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre

Bio: Dr. Hannah Fair has two overlapping focuses: the role of social networks in dementia risk reduction, and understanding and improving equity in health promotion, particularly in dementia prevention. She evaluates online health education programs like the ISLAND project Linking Aging and Neurodegenerative Disease, and the Preventing Dementia Massive Open Online Course, to assessing their impact and reach through mixed-methods research. Dr. Fair also explores the role of social networks in transmitting dementia risk information and behaviour, and is increasingly interested in the broader role of social networks in promoting dementia risk reducing behaviour. Her research methods involve both quantitative (statistical modelling, social network analysis) and qualitative (interviews, focus groups, thematic analysis) approaches. She teaches on public health approaches to dementia and dementia risk reduction, emphasizing health equity and social determinants of health. Dr. Hannah Fair works for the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre at the University of Tasmania, and welcomes any and all conversations with individuals who share her interests.

Bio: Dr Hongyuan Liu is currently a senior lecturer in geomechanics at the School of Engineering in the College of Sciences and Engineering, University of Tasmania and an affiliated research scientist at CSIRO Mineral Resources. Hong's research interest is in the field of geohazard mitigation and prevention, computational geomechanics, tunnelling, and rock mechanics. In particular, Hong's research focuses on the development and application of advanced computational methods such as hybrid finite-discrete element method (HFDEM) in studying the fracture and fragmentation of rocks under various static and dynamic loads during tunnelling and mining, associated microseismicities, and their interactions with underground fluids such as groundwater, oil, gas and hazardous waste as well as mitigating and even preventing geohazards such as rockbursts, slope instabilities and iceberg calving. Role: Doctor

School: Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies

Sub-organisation: Ecology and Biodiversity

Bio: Dr Jane Younger is a Senior Lecturer in Southern Ocean Vertebrate Ecology at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS). Her research integrates an Antarctic field program with cutting edge multi-omics approaches to monitor the complex impacts of climate change on Antarctic biodiversity, with a particular focus on understanding the threat of disease to wildlife in a changing environment. She is a 2025-26 Science and Technology Australia Superstar of STEM, a Senior Editor of Ecology and Evolution, a National Geographic Explorer, and a 2025 Young Tall Poppy Award winner.Prior to joining IMAS in 2022, Jane was a research fellow in the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath (UK). Her research focused on understanding the impacts of climate change on seabirds, through an evolutionary lens. She has also held an Endeavour Fellowship at the University of Oxford (UK) where she used genomics to examine the population structure of Southern Ocean penguin species. Prior to that she held a postdoctoral position at Loyola University Chicago (USA) and in affiliation with the Field Museum of Natural History, studying the evolution of Madagascar’s endemic avifauna.

Role: Doctor

School: School of Humanities

Bio: Dr Jayne Knight is Senior Lecturer in Classics and Associate Head of School, Learning and Teaching Performance in the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. She researches the emotional culture of ancient Rome, with a particular focus on how emotions shaped politics and rhetoric in the late Republic and early Empire. Her monograph Anger and Politics in Ancient Rome (Bloomsbury, 2026) is the centrepiece of this program, building on her earlier work including ‘Anger as a Mechanism for Social Control in Imperial Rome’ in Emotion and Persuasion in Classical Antiquity (Franz Steiner Verlag, 2016), and connecting with forthcoming chapters on ‘Emotions in Roman Oratory’ in A Companion to Ancient Rhetoric: New Trends and Interdisciplinary Perspectives (De Gruyter, expected 2026) and ‘Senecan Strategies for Managing Envy in Early Imperial Rome’ for a planned volume on Envy in the Roman World (University of Michigan Press). Her entries on ‘emotions’ and ‘hatred’ in The Tacitus Encyclopedia (Wiley-Blackwell, 2023) further reflect her interest in the affective dimensions of Roman historical writing.

Imperial Rome’ for a planned volume on Envy in the Roman World (University of Michigan Press). Her entries on ‘emotions’ and ‘hatred’ in The Tacitus Encyclopedia (Wiley-Blackwell, 2023) further reflect her interest in the affective dimensions of Roman historical writing.

A second strand of her research examines how Roman thought on politics and emotions was received and transformed in later periods. Her ARC-funded project on Machiavelli's engagement with Roman political theory informs a forthcoming chapter on ‘Anger and Discord in Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy’ in Machiavelli and the Anatomy of Passions (Brill). Her chapter ‘The Nature and Nurture of Kingship in Virgil's Georgics and Seneca's De Clementia’ in Latin Poetry and its Reception (Routledge, 2021) analyses Seneca's engagement with earlier Virgilian ideas and imagery to activate historical memory.

Jayne believes that ancient texts speak to deep questions of human life, and one of the most rewarding things Classics can do is help students experience and appreciate the deep connections and gulfs between the ancient world and their own. Bio: Jessica Urwin is Lecturer in Environmental History in the School of Humanities, College of Arts, Law and Education. Her research interests and expertise span nuclear history, Australian history, environmental history, colonial and imperial history, and environmental justice. Her award-winning doctoral research, completed at the Australian National University, explored the relationship between nuclear processes (including radium and uranium mining, nuclear weapons testing, and nuclear waste dumping) and colonialism in Australia. Her first monograph, Contaminated Country: Nuclear Colonialism and Aboriginal Resistance in Australia, was published in the University of Washington Press' Weyehaeuser Environmental Books series in September 2025 and an Australian edition is set to be published by Melbourne University Press in 2026.

Jess is a member of the Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand Environmental History Network's steering committee, an editorial board member of Global Environment, and a Friend of the Centre for Environmental History at ANU.

Research Interests

Jess' research interests span across Australian scientific, environmental, political, and colonial history. Her immediate field of expertise is in Australian nuclear, colonial, and environmental histories, but she has also worked on historical research

Research Interests

Jess' research interests span across Australian scientific, environmental, political, and colonial history. Her immediate field of expertise is in Australian nuclear, colonial, and environmental histories, but she has also worked on historical research concerned with the Murray-Darling Basin and other 'watery spaces', oral history, global environmental history, and the history of science and scientific networks in Australia and beyond.

Expanding upon her work into nuclear colonialism, Jess is interested in Australian mining history, and hopes to engage critically with the industry's environmental and colonial dimensions, from settlement through to the present. In particular, she is interested in the politics of mineral extraction, from understanding the 'roots' of settlers' engagements with mining (in particular of radioactive minerals), to tracing the 'routes' of mined minerals across the world, to grappling with mining's more recent interactions with Indigenous land rights and conservation debates.

Bio: Dr Johanna Jones is a postdoctoral researcher at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research. After working in the education sector for several years, Johanna undertook additional study to complement her interests in health and human disease. She has a great interest in understanding how genetic variants disrupt normal cell biology and lead to disease. Johanna’s research is primarily focused on the genetics of childhood onset (congenital/paediatric) cataracts. She was awarded a PhD in 2020 from the University of Tasmania in the genetics of paediatric cataract. This successful body of work identified PGRMC1 as a novel isolated cataract gene, expanded the genotype-phenotype spectrum of known cataract genes, and has initiated investigations into the importance of structural and non-coding variants in cataract genetics. Johanna has honed a broad range of skills from sequencing and bioinformatics for variant identification and prioritisation, through numerous molecular biology techniques and use of zebrafish as a cataract disease model for variant validation and functional assessments. Johanna is also interested in developing in vitro assays to test the functional effects of

Johanna is also interested in developing in vitro assays to test the functional effects of putative disease-causing variants to improve genetic testing outcomes for patients. embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor Juan Afonso

Role: Doctor

School: University of Tasmania

Sub-organisation: Earth Sciences/CODES

Bio: A/Prof. Juan C. Afonso's background is in computational geoscience and geodata integration. After graduating with a PhD in theoretical geophysics at Carleton University, Juan C. Afonso undertook postdoctoral research at the Institute of Earth Sciences Jaume Almera (CSIC, Barcelona) on the development of new methods to study the thermal and compositional structures of the lithospheric/sublithospheric upper mantle. He subsequently joined Macquarie University in 2009 as part of the recruitment program CoRE (Concentration of Research Excellence). In 2022, he joined the ITC Faculty (University of Twente, Netherlands) as full-time staff. In 2026 he joined the School of Natural Sciences at the University of Tasmania. He was an Adjunct Professor at the Centre for Earth Evolution and Dynamics (CEED, University of Oslo) and Honorary Professor at the Dept. of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Macquarie University. He currently is a Visiting Professor in the Department of Earth and Space Sciences at SUSTech University and in ITC at the University of Twente.

Dr Afonso's

embedding_items.title: Doctor Juan Afonso
embedding_items.text:
Honorary Professor at the Dept. of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Macquarie University. He currently is a Visiting Professor in the Department of Earth and Space Sciences at SUSTech University and in ITC at the University of Twente.

Dr Afonso's current research includes the development of methodologies (and associated computational tools) that formally combine geophysics, numerical modelling, petrology and geochemistry to obtain reliable and realistic models of the Earth's interior using satellite-derived and land-based data sets. For this (and related) work he has received the 2013 EGU Outstanding Young Scientist Award (Geodynamics Division), the 2017 Anton Hales Medal of the Australian Academy of Sciences and the 2019 IUGG Early Career Scientist Award, among others.

His research centers on understanding the thermochemical structure and evolution of the lithosphere, as well as the mechanical and geochemical interactions between tectonic plates and the sublithospheric upper mantle. His work explores how these interactions influence both regional and global tectonic processes, with implications for plate dynamics, mantle convection, and crustal evolution.
​​
His most recent research integrates machine learning, multiscale probabilistic inversion, and numerical modeling to investigate

​​
His most recent research integrates machine learning, multiscale probabilistic inversion, and numerical modeling to investigate some of the most fundamental questions about the nature and evolution of the lithosphere and upper mantle using a formal combination of multiple satellite (e.g. gravity, magnetic field) and land-based (e.g. geochemistry, seismic) data sets.
​​
He also works on the development of novel numerical algorithms to model the complex coupling between geodynamic and geochemical processes. This work directly supports the global energy transition by enabling more accurate and physically realistic models for geothermal resource assessment and critical mineral exploration. His methodologies assist in identifying subsurface conditions favorable for sustainable energy development and securing the raw materials essential for clean energy technologies.

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Karelle Siellez is an astrophysicist and Lecturer in Physics at the University of Tasmania. Her research focuses on transient and multi-messenger astrophysics, including gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae, supernovae, gravitational-wave counterparts, and rapid optical follow-up of short-lived cosmic explosions. Her work connects high-energy space missions, gravitational-wave observatories, and ground-based telescope networks to understand some of the most energetic events in the Universe.
Before joining UTAS, Dr Siellez contributed to major international collaborations including LIGO/Virgo and Fermi/GBM. She developed and led work on subthreshold gamma-ray burst searches associated with gravitational-wave events, contributing to the scientific context of the first joint gravitational-wave and electromagnetic detection, GW170817/GRB 170817A. This discovery transformed the field by confirming that neutron-star mergers can produce both gravitational waves and light, and that they are sites of heavy-element production in the Universe. As part of the LIGO Scientific Collaboration, she shared in the 2017 Breakthrough Prize in

At UTAS, Dr Siellez is developing a research, teaching and engagement program centred on southern-hemisphere transient astronomy. Her work aims to strengthen the role of Tasmanian optical facilities in rapid follow-up of gamma-ray bursts, kilonovae and gravitational-wave counterparts, while creating student pathways into real astronomical research. She is involved in national and international initiatives linked to SVOM, Rubin Observatory/LSST, OzGrav, robotic telescope networks and time-domain astronomy.
Dr Siellez is also a committed science communicator who connects physics with storytelling, music, visual art and public engagement. She has delivered public talks and outreach activities across Australia, France, French Polynesia and the United States, including schools, festivals, public lectures and interdisciplinary science-art events. Her engagement work includes gravitational-wave sonification, astronomy-inspired painting, dark-sky advocacy, and public programs highlighting the scientific, cultural and environmental importance of Tasmania’s skies.

Bio: Dr Karen Hall is a lecturer in art at the School of Creative and Performing Arts at the Inveresk campus. My research explores connections between past and present within the Tasmanian landscape, examining the interplay of cultural and environmental changes through her individual practice and collaborative projects. I reach in a range of areas, from art and performance theory and histories to the material and visual cultures of family history. I have led significant curriculum change and prioritise inclusion through my teaching.

I completed my PhD at the University of Western Australia in 2008. Joining the then School of Visual and Performing Arts, I developed and delivered new units in art and performance history and theory. I am currently the Graduate Research Coordinator for the School of Creative and Performing Arts.

I am the Tasmanian representative for the Art Association for Australia and New Zealand.

embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor Ke Liu

Role: Doctor

Bio: Dr Ke Liu has established an internationally recognised research profile in climate adaptation science and agricultural systems modelling. His work has significantly advanced the representation of soil waterlogging stress in many farming systems models, repositioning waterlogging from a historically under-represented agronomic constraint to a quantifiable and scenario-testable climate risk within mainstream process-based crop modelling frameworks. He led the development and implementation of generic waterlogging algorithms within internationally recognised modelling platforms (APSIM Classic/Next Generation, DSSAT and SWAGMAN Destiny), enabling cross-regional and scenario-based risk quantification. These tools have been adopted within collaborative modelling programs and decision-support frameworks used in more than 30 countries, supporting improved assessment of soil waterlogging stress in climate impact analyses.
His 2023 Nature Communications paper, “Silver lining to a climate crisis in multiple prospects for alleviating crop waterlogging under future climates,” provided the first global-scale quantification of current and future waterlogging risk and mitigation potential and has helped catalyse broader research attention to waterlogging risk in climate impact assessments. This paper was featured by the journal under its Earth and Environmental

This paper was featured by the journal under its Earth and Environmental Sciences Highlights and has been cited over 250 times and recognised as a Highly Cited Paper in the Web of Science. In recognition of the study’s significant impact, Dr. Liu was invited by the Nature editorial team to create a popular science video in 2024. The video has garnered more than 15,000 views on YouTube, reflecting the broad interest and influence of his research within the scientific community.
Dr Liu has also been invited to co-lead the AgMIP waterlogging initiative, a leading international platform dedicated to harmonising soil waterlogging stress representation across crop models. This collaboration culminated in a Nature Food review, “Gaps and strategies for accurate simulation of waterlogging impacts on crop productivity”, published in 2025, which identified key knowledge gaps and strategic pathways for advancing waterlogging simulation and modelling standards internationally, further advancing the global understanding and modeling of waterlogging effects on agricultural systems.

Bio: Dr Kyra Wood is an experienced academic and research project manager with a professional background in architecture and design. Role: Doctor

School: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Sub-organisation: Menzies Institute for Medical Research

Bio: Dr Lieke Scheepers is a Research Fellow in the Environmental and Respiratory Health group at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research, University of Tasmania. She is an epidemiologist specialising in how early‑life environmental exposures influence health and development from pregnancy through to childhood and later life.

Her research focuses on a range of environmental exposures, including ambient air pollution, wildfire smoke, greenness, and pesticide exposure. Using a life‑course epidemiology approach, her work examines how these exposures affect pregnancy outcomes, birth, and long‑term health trajectories. Her research draws on large cohort studies and data linkage to generate robust evidence grounded in real‑world health outcomes, to inform prevention strategies and public‑health policy.

Dr Scheepers is the Lead of the Early‑Life Follow‑up (ELF) Stream of the Hazelwood Health Study, where she investigates the long-term cardiorespiratory, health and development of children exposed to a severe pollution event associated with a coal mine fire during their first 1000 days of life.

She also provides scientific and operational leadership for the Statins Against Bushfire Smoke (SABS) clinical trial, which is testing whether interventions can reduce the cardiovascular impacts of wildfire smoke exposure.
She is always interested in hearing from motivated Honours and PhD students who would like to work on environmental exposures and early‑life health using large population datasets.

Bio: Luca is a marine geoscientist. He obtained his PhD from the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) at the University of Tasmania, where his research investigated the post-emplacement rifting of oceanic Large Igneous Provinces.

In 2024, Luca joined the EarthByte Group at the University of Sydney as a Postdoctoral Fellow, working on the tectonic evolution of the Coral Sea and the development of global datasets for the validation of palaeo-elevation reconstructions. He subsequently joined IMAS as a Research Associate, where he focuses on marine and Antarctic geophysics.

Luca's research interests focus predominantly on marine geophysics, plate tectonics, ocean basin evolution, scientific ocean drilling, geodynamics, and sedimentology. Bio: Dr McCallum is an expert in the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique. 'In VLBI we use signals from far distant radio galaxies to measure the Earth. In more detail, VLBI is used to measure the Earth's shape, the rotation of the Earth, polar motion, plate tectonics and the variation of these effects.'Dr. McCallum is the project scientist in the AuScope VLBI project, a research collaboration with Geoscience Australia, as part of the Positioning Australia project. She uses the university's own radio telescopes at Mt. Pleasant, the Northern Territory and in Western Australia, in common measurements together with telescopes all over the world. The goals of the VLBI group at UTAS are to guarantee best possible performance of our telescopes in global observations and to develop new methods to implement the next generation VLBI global observing system (VGOS). VGOS will be able to measure global distances to the level of a few millimetres, a necessity for important scientific and societal questions in geosciences, as for example the prediction of sea level rise of a few

Dr McCallum’s research focuses in the field of space ties, meaning that she tries to connect the geodetic techniques of the Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS, GPS), Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) and VLBI directly via a single satellite platform. Essential for space ties is VLBI satellite tracking. Bio: Dr Lydia Mackenzie is a Lecturer in Biogeography and Conservation at the University of Tasmania. Her research focuses on paleoenvironmental indicators, environmental geochemistry, and paleoecology. She uses a range of proxies to understand terrestrial and aquatic ecosystem dynamics, past climate change, and the long-term relationship between humans and the environment. Lydia's research incorporates pollen, phytoliths, charcoal, radioisotopes, sedimentology, and micro-XRF geochemical analysis. Her research projects are currently focused on alpine ecosystems in both Australia and northern China.

Find out more about the Palaeoecology and Biogeography Lab at UTas here.

Bio: Dr Nicholas Blackburn is a Senior Research Fellow in Computational Genomics at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research. First as a postdoctoral fellow and then as a faculty member he conducted genomics based research, primarily in large multigenerational families, into complex diseases and quantitative phenotypes. He uses his genomics expertise to provide support to a wide range of studies in the institute while growing his own research into complex disease – with a current focus on multiple sclerosis.In 2022 Dr Blackburn was awarded a fellowship from MS Australia to investigate rare genetic variation in multiple sclerosis.

Bio: Dr Nicholas Hookway – sometimes known as the ‘happy sociologist’ – is Senior Lecturer in Sociology in the School of Social Sciences. Nick is a cultural sociologist whose research focuses on how social bonds, emotions and identity are being transformed by wider social change. He is internationally known for his research on kindness, everyday morality, sports charity, loneliness and digital methods. From Toyota to Cancer Council Tasmania, Nick’s research has led to successful partnerships with a range of local and national organisations. Nick has published in the best sociology journals in the world, including Sociology, British Journal of Sociology, The Sociological Review and Qualitative Research. His monograph Everyday Moralities: Doing it Ourselves in an Age of Uncertainty was awarded the prestigious Stephen Crook Memorial Prize (2020) for best book in Australian sociology. Nick is a leader in developing digital methods in sociology. His article on using blogs in social research has been cited over 1000 times. Nick was an elected member of The Australian Sociology Association (TASA) Executive Committee (Public Engagement Portfolio Leader) (2016–2020) and prior to this was the Co-Convenor of the Cultural Sociology TASA Thematic Group

Bio: Peter is a Lecturer in the School of Architecture & Design at the University of Tasmania, specialising in computational design, digital fabrication, and sustainable material-driven approaches to architectural innovation. As an Early Career Researcher (ECR), his research investigates how emerging digital workflows can more effectively integrate material behaviour, fabrication constraints, and sustainability principles to advance architectural practice and regional manufacturing capacity. His work particularly emphasises the potential of latent wood-based materials within digitally integrated design and manufactured workflows.

Peter has more than two decades of combined professional and academic experience within the field of architecture. Since registering as an architect in 2005, he has worked across Tasmania, Melbourne, and London in roles that include Project Architect on residential, commercial, heritage, healthcare, and educational projects. In 2012, he co‑founded Pulp Studio Architecture, where he continues to serve as Director, contributing design leadership and technical expertise to residential and small‑scale commercial work.

Bio: Dr Rachel Climie is an NHMRC Emerging Leader, Heart Foundation Future Leader Fellow and Clinical Exercise Physiologist. Rachel's research is focused on primordial prevention (the prevention of risk factor onset) of cardiovascular disease, commencing in early life. Rachel and her team are developing ways to identify young people at risk of premature heart disease and working with local communities to develop solutions to minimise this risk. Rachel completed her PhD at the Menzies Institute for Medical Research in 2016. She then undertook 2 years postdoctoral research studying cardiovascular epidemiology and arterial mechanics at Paris Research Center Cardiovasculaire (PARCC), France, where she is an Honorary Fellow. Rachel was awarded a Heart Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship (and Paul Korner Award) to work with the Sports Cardiology research team at the Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute, before returning to Tasmania in 2021.

Bio: Ross Turner is a Lecturer in Mathematics and Physics at the University of Tasmania. He received the University of Tasmania's Vice Chancellor's Award in 2022 for his accomplishments as an early career researcher, and was a finalist for the Australian Museum Eureka Prize in the same year for his outreach work at QueersInScience. Ross has previously been awarded the prestigious Bok Prize by the Astronomical Society of Australia for his theoretical astrophysics research on the relativistic jet outflows from supermassive black holes.

Ross leads the analytical modelling research stream in the University's Theoretical and Computational Astrophysics Group (physics/astrophysics), which develops the statistical tools to analyse radio astronomy observations from next-generation large sky surveys, including by the Square Kilometre Array. He employs his expertise in computational physics to model and interpret complex dynamical systems as part of cross-disciplinary research with the Australian Centre for Excellence in Antarctic Science (computational earth sciences) and the Climate Mathematics Group (applied mathematics).

Bio: I am a marine scientist specialising in fisheries assessment, population ecology, and spatial data analysis. I routinely provide science-based advice to government and industry through technical reports, working groups, and briefings.

My expertise spans stock assessment methods including CPUE standardization, surplus production models (CMSY, BSM, OCOM), and statistical modelling using GAMs and GLMs. I am highly proficient in R programming for data analysis and visualization, and experienced with GIS platforms (ArcGIS, QGIS) for spatial analysis of marine populations and fisheries.

My earlier career centered on marine vertebrate ecology, particularly the movements, habitat use, and population dynamics of seals and seabirds in relation to offshore energy infrastructure. embedding_items.text:
Supervisor: Doctor Ryan Day

Role: Doctor

Bio: Ryan Day is Senior Research Fellow in Marine Animal Physiology and Biochemistry at University of Tasmania’s Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. In 2003, he received a Bachelor of Arts - Biology from the University of Chicago. In 2006, he received a Bachelor of Science - Marine Biology from the University of Queensland and in 2012, he received his PhD in Zoology from the University of Queensland.

Ryan has been a researcher at IMAS since 2012. One of his primary research areas are in measuring the impact of seismic surveys on marine invertebrates. In this field, his research has used quantification of acid-base physiology, haemolymph electrolyte and mineral homeostasis, immune function and oxidative stress to assess the health status of marine invertebrates including lobster, scallops and octopus to evaluate the impact of exposure to seismic air gun signals. The outcomes of this research have been incorporated by the federal regulatory body (NOPSEMA) for impact assessments to minimise harm to marine life.

In his second primary research area, Ryan investigates approaches for improving invertebrate fishery practices and outcomes, with a current focus on the commercial scallop. This research developed in response to reports of large-scale mortalities

embedding_items.title: Doctor Ryan Day
embedding_items.text:
to minimise harm to marine life.

In his second primary research area, Ryan investigates approaches for improving invertebrate fishery practices and outcomes, with a current focus on the commercial scallop. This research developed in response to reports of large-scale mortalities within the scallop fishery. In conducting an assessment of haemolymph physiology, including biochemistry and immune function, his research aims to identify environmental stressors underlying mortality to provide fishery management with options for responding to bed die offs. In similar work with the Southern Rock Lobster fishery response, Ryan authored an industry best practices guide with recommendations on handling and water quality management. Implementation of these recommendations has been attributed to eliminating mass mortality events and halving mortality rates by industry partners. This work has recently been extended to the fishing vessel component of the industry and projects to apply this research to other marine invertebrate fisheries are in development. In addition to his recent work with invertebrates, Ryan’s PhD research focused on digestive physiology in marine fishes, in which he characterised digestive strategies in fishes that lack a stomach.

Thopate ignited his passion for synthetic organic chemistry, particularly for organic reaction mechanisms. Rising from a below-average student to one of the top three in his class at the New Arts, Commerce, and Science College, Parner, he also ranked 5th in Chemistry across all colleges under the University of Pune in 2009.

Bio: I am a nursing academic researcher in the fields of palliative care and aged care and an active member of the Transforming Research in Ageing (TRiA) group within the school of Nursing at the University of Tasmania. My research and teaching areas focus on workforce education and skills development in palliative care, and care and quality of life of older people. I joined the project team on the first Australian-funded research study into the benefits of the multisensory, psychosocial Namaste Care program for people living with advanced dementia in residential aged care facilities and continue to promote the program’s philosophy and principles into various contexts of care as the Australian champion for Namaste Care International. My focus is on developing skilled, compassionate palliative care nurses (and care staff) within aged care and nursing graduands who are invested in evidence-informed practice. I endeavour to set students up for success as nurses of the future by helping to transmit evidence-based knowledge, develop comprehensive assessment skills and encourage positive, empowering attitudes so that they can provide the care that health and social care providers, patients, residents, clients and their families

BiographySara’s background embraces both the Arts and Science. As a Classics graduate from the University of London, Sara worked in educational publishing before undertaking a Bachelor of Nursing at the University of Technology, Sydney and beginning her nursing career. During this time, she identified her interest in palliative care, from which specialisation she could explore the perenial questions surrounding living and dying, health and ill health, and what matters as we face ageing and dying. An output of Sara's Bachelor of Nursing studies was a chapter 'Spirituality in Palliative Care' written within a resource for nurse practitioners entering the speciality of palliative care.

Sara’s clinical background is palliative care nursing across specialist, acute and community palliative care services. Sara’s PhD (2018) research focused on the residential aged care workforce and the development of an instrument to evaluate the knowledge, skills and attitudes of nursing assistants (unlicensed health care workers) providing a palliative approach to older

Sara joined the University of Tasmania as a Lecturer in Nursing in August 2017 and teaches into both the undergraduate and postgraduate programs.

Bio: Dr. Sheree Armistead is an Australian Research Council DECRA fellow at CODES (Centre for Ore Deposit and Earth Sciences), where she investigates the interplay between plate tectonics and mineral systems, focusing on their cyclical and long-term changes throughout Earth’s history. Her expertise spans isotope geochemistry, data science, GIS, and plate reconstruction techniques to unravel the processes that shape mineral systems over geological timescales.

Sheree's DECRA fellowship is titled The interplay of tectonics and climate on critical minerals in deep time. This project seeks to address the urgent need for critical minerals by identifying tectonic and climatic conditions favorable for forming sediment-hosted copper and cobalt deposits over the last billion years. Using samples from the Central African Copperbelt—the world’s largest sediment-hosted Cu-Co district—alongside cutting-edge plate tectonic models, global sedimentary basin datasets, and geochemical tools, this research aims to provide innovative predictive frameworks for locating ore deposits in Australia and globally.

Sheree joined UTAS as a Postdoctoral Researcher and Lecturer in

sediment-hosted Cu-Co district—alongside cutting-edge plate tectonic models, global sedimentary basin datasets, and geochemical tools, this research aims to provide innovative predictive frameworks for locating ore deposits in Australia and globally.

Sheree joined UTAS as a Postdoctoral Researcher and Lecturer in 2022, where she has led and contributed to several research projects, including a collaborative project with Geoscience Australia on the tectonic and metallogenic evolution of western Tasmania. Her work bridges the gap between fundamental geoscience research and its practical applications in mineral exploration.

Before joining UTAS, Sheree undertook a two-year Postdoctoral Research Fellowship at the Geological Survey of Canada in Ottawa, funded through the Metal Earth program at Laurentian University. This project used a global database of Pb isotopes from ore deposits to understand early Earth geodynamics and plate tectonics, with implications for ore-forming regions, particularly the Superior Province in Canada.

This work contributed to refining global plate reconstructions spanning the past billion years.

Bio: Dr. Tamieka Pearce is a Research Fellow at the Tasmanian Institute of Agriculture (TIA), specialising in genetics and molecular plant pathology. Her work underpins the productivity and sustainability of Tasmania’s horticultural industries. Since completing her PhD in 2016, she has focused on plant disease research in crops including pyrethrum, poppies, cherries, and blueberries. Her research has attracted more than $3.6 million in funding, with a third of this secured through projects she has led as Chief Investigator.
Tamieka currently leads a pyrethrum flowering physiology research program aimed at reducing the crop growing season from 18 months to 10 months. This program integrates the identification of early-flowering plants, assessment of heritability, development of tissue culture techniques, and the use of genomic and transcriptome analyses to identify candidate genes in the juvenile–adult transition pathway. In 2023, she was awarded an ARC Early Career Industry Fellowship to advance this research, becoming the only UTAS recipient in the inaugural fellowship round.

He actively works for the Maritime Infrastructure Integrity and Environment (MarIInE) Laboratory, which enables the assessment of the structural integrity of maritime assets and their relationship and impacts on the marine environment. He also completed a Bachelor of Engineering (Marine & Offshore Engineering) with Honors from the same institution in 2014. Bio: Crop physiologist and research leader with expertise in sustainable agriculture, climate resilience, and plant nitrogen and carbon assimilation.
My research focuses on developing strategies to improve crop performance, nutrient use efficiency, and sustainability under future climate conditions. I lead multidisciplinary collaborations that integrate crop physiology, molecular biology, and systems-based approaches to address climate and emissions challenges in Australian agriculture.
Currently, I lead industry-engaged programs through the Tasmanian Institute of Agriculture, including projects on Zero Net Emissions Horticulture, climate adaptation in legumes, and sustainable crop protection technologies. Recognised through a Tall Poppy Award, I am committed to translating science into impact through partnership, innovation, and capacity building.
